cards.gloss: Three core metrics for recruitment cost
cards.verbatim: The true cost of recruitment is typically measured through three interlocking metrics: cost-per-hire (CPH), time-to-fill, and cost-of-vacancy (COV), each capturing a different dimension of what an open position actually costs an organization.

cards.gloss: CPH is the most standardized metric
cards.verbatim: Cost-per-hire is the most standardized of the three.

cards.gloss: CPH formula codified in 2012 by SHRM/ANSI
cards.verbatim: The formula was formally codified in 2012 through a joint effort between the Society for Human Resource Management (SHRM) and the American National Standards Institute (ANSI)[1].

cards.gloss: SHRM/ANSI definition of CPH
cards.verbatim: The SHRM/ANSI standard defines CPH as "the mean average of total costs divided by the number of hires"[1]

cards.gloss: CPH cost components: internal vs external
cards.verbatim: encompassing both internal costs (recruiter time, internal systems) and external costs (agency fees, job board postings, advertising) incurred to fill open positions[1]

cards.gloss: LinkedIn's CPH definition
cards.verbatim: LinkedIn's recruiting metrics guide offers a consistent definition: total spend associated with filling an open position (recruiter fees, advertisements, etc.) divided by the number of hires[1].

cards.gloss: Time-to-fill vs time-to-hire often conflated
cards.verbatim: Time-to-fill and time-to-hire are related but distinct time-based indicators that are frequently conflated.

cards.gloss: Time-to-fill definition
cards.verbatim: Time-to-fill measures the number of days between when a job requisition is opened or approved and when a candidate accepts the offer (in some organizations, when the new hire starts)[2][3]

cards.gloss: 2024 time-to-fill benchmark: 54 days
cards.verbatim: The 2024 benchmark for time-to-fill is approximately 54 days[2].

cards.gloss: Cost-of-vacancy definition
cards.verbatim: Cost-of-vacancy (COV) quantifies the cost of leaving a position unfilled

cards.gloss: COV factors depend on position, industry, lifecycle stage
cards.verbatim: and the underlying factors that determine it are largely dependent on the position, the industry, and the current stage of the product lifecycle[4].

cards.gloss: Average revenue per lost employee calculation
cards.verbatim: **Average revenue per lost employee**: a company's total revenue divided by its number of employees, then divided by the number of working days in a year (220), yielding the average daily revenue an employee generates — revenue that is not produced while the position sits vacant[4].

cards.gloss: Salary multiplier of revenue lost calculation
cards.verbatim: **Salary multiplier of revenue lost**: a calculation based on the premise of lost revenue relative to the position's salary[4].

cards.gloss: Advice to build COV formula with finance department
cards.verbatim: Organizations building a COV formula are advised to develop it in conjunction with the finance department

cards.gloss: Levers exist to reduce recruitment time and cost
cards.verbatim: Several levers are commonly cited as reducing both the time and cost dimensions of recruitment:

cards.gloss: Employee referrals as a lever
cards.verbatim: encouraging internal employee referrals, which are a cost-effective sourcing channel and tend to produce higher-quality hires who align with company culture[5]

cards.gloss: Optimizing job descriptions as a lever
cards.verbatim: optimizing job descriptions to attract genuinely qualified candidates and reduce time spent sorting irrelevant resumes[5]

cards.gloss: Pre-employment assessments as a lever
cards.verbatim: using pre-employment assessments to gauge candidate skills and fit, reducing the risk of a bad hire[5]

cards.gloss: Automating recruitment tasks as a lever
cards.verbatim: automating repetitive recruitment tasks such as resume screening, interview scheduling, and follow-up messaging[2]

cards.gloss: Maintaining a warm talent pipeline as a lever
cards.verbatim: maintaining an active, warm talent pipeline through talent communities and proactive sourcing rather than starting to source only after a requisition is approved[2]

cards.gloss: Definition of cost of vacancy (COV)
cards.verbatim: Cost of vacancy (COV) is the metric used to quantify the actual business impact of a talent shortage created by the gap between when a role is needed and when the recruiting function can fill it[4].

cards.gloss: What COV can be configured to measure
cards.verbatim: It can be configured to measure the dollar impact of voluntary and involuntary turnover, or the impact of a recruiting process too slow to meet an organization's growing talent needs[4].

cards.gloss: COV has no standardized formula, unlike CPH
cards.verbatim: Unlike cost-per-hire, there is no magic or standardized formula for calculating cost of vacancy, because the factors involved vary by role and organization[4].

cards.gloss: Simplified estimation used except for key roles
cards.verbatim: Many organizations therefore use a simplified estimation formula rather than calculating the true, fully-loaded cost for every position, reserving detailed calculation for key roles[4].

cards.gloss: COV range $7k-$12k/day, up to $200k/day for time-to-market critical roles
cards.verbatim: In roles where time-to-market is a critical driver of corporate success, the cost of a single vacancy has been calculated at between $7,000 and $12,000 per day, and in one documented case reached as high as $200,000 per day[4].

cards.gloss: Simplified $100/day vacancy-productivity-loss estimate
cards.verbatim: One source ties a simplified vacancy-productivity-loss estimate to roughly $100 per day the role remains unfilled[6]

cards.gloss: Example: 45-day open sales role costs $112,500 in lost revenue
cards.verbatim: illustrates the scale effect with a senior sales role left open for 45 days costing an estimated $112,500 in lost revenue[7].

cards.gloss: CPH codified in 2012 by SHRM/ANSI
cards.verbatim: It was codified in 2012 through a joint effort between the Society for Human Resource Management (SHRM) and the American National Standards Institute (ANSI), which defines CPH as "the mean average of total costs divided by the number of hires"[1].

cards.gloss: The Cost Per Hire formula
cards.verbatim: Cost Per Hire = (Total Internal Costs + Total External Costs) ÷ Total Number of Hires[1][8][7]

cards.gloss: CPH formula is consistent but implementation varies
cards.verbatim: While the fundamental formula is consistent across these sources, implementation is not: some organizations exclude indirect costs like hiring managers' time for simplicity, while others include onboarding costs even though this is not standard practice

cards.gloss: Recommendation to document CPH methodology for comparability
cards.verbatim: making it important for organizations to document their exact CPH methodology so comparisons stay apples-to-apples[1].

cards.gloss: Internal CPH cost components
cards.verbatim: Internal cost components typically include recruiting staff salaries and benefits (fully loaded cost of in-house recruiters and talent acquisition team members), prorated salaries of HR staff or hiring managers for interviewing/recruiting time, recruiting department overhead (office infrastructure, equipment, compliance costs), and internal sourcing costs such as employee referral bonuses[1][8].

cards.gloss: External CPH cost components
cards.verbatim: External costs include job board fees, agency fees, advertising, background checks, drug testing, skills assessments, and candidate travel expenses[8][6].

cards.gloss: Direct vs indirect cost split, indirect is 60-70% of true total
cards.verbatim: One source separates these into "direct costs" (job advertising, agency fees, background checks, assessments — the costs most commonly tracked) versus "indirect costs," which it estimates make up 60–70% of the true total and include manager/team interview time, productivity loss during the vacancy period, administrative processing, onboarding and training, equipment/software setup, and the productivity gap during new-hire ramp-up[6].

cards.gloss: 2026 guide: teams undercount CPH by omitting hidden costs
cards.verbatim: A 2026 guide notes that most teams still undercount CPH because they omit manager time leakage, tool-stack bloat, no-show interviews, and the productivity hit of an unfilled seat

cards.gloss: Example: $3,000 vs $10,000+ per hire gap explained by inputs not formula
cards.verbatim: explaining why two companies hiring similar roles can report $3,000 vs. $10,000+ per hire, since it is the inputs rather than the formula that explain the gap[9].

cards.gloss: Worked example: $8,000 CPH from $400,000/50 hires
cards.verbatim: A company that spent $300,000 on internal costs and $100,000 on external costs to hire 50 people has a cost per hire of $8,000 ($400,000 ÷ 50)[8].

cards.gloss: Worked example: $6,000 CPH from $60,000/10 hires
cards.verbatim: A business spending $60,000 on hiring activities in one quarter while bringing on 10 new employees has a cost per hire of $6,000 ($60,000 ÷ 10)[10].

cards.gloss: Worked example: $4,700 CPH from 5 October hires
cards.verbatim: Five hires made in October with $7,000 in internal costs and $16,500 in external costs yields $4,700 per hire (($7,000 + $16,500) ÷ 5)[11].

cards.gloss: Worked example: $1,875 CPH from 40-person company, 8 roles
cards.verbatim: A 40-person company filling 8 roles in a quarter with $6,000 in external costs (job board posts, background checks, one contingency agency fee) and $9,000 in internal costs (hiring manager and recruiter time) yields $1,875 per hire (($6,000 + $9,000) ÷ 8)[9].

cards.gloss: Recommended practice: quarterly cadence for gathering cost data
cards.verbatim: gather cost data from finance reports and HR systems for a chosen time period (quarterly is described as the most practical cadence — enough volume for a useful number without waiting too long to spot a trend)

cards.gloss: Recommended practice: cross-reference totals against accounting records
cards.verbatim: cross-reference totals against accounting records for accuracy

cards.gloss: Recommended practice: count whole hires, not fractional FTEs
cards.verbatim: count whole hires rather than fractional full-time-equivalents

cards.gloss: Recommended practice: avoid mismatched cost/hire periods
cards.verbatim: avoid comparing costs and hires from mismatched periods (e.g., annual costs against monthly hires)[8][9]

cards.gloss: CPH benchmarks vary by source/year/scope
cards.verbatim: Reported average CPH figures vary by source and year, reflecting differing scope and survey timing.

cards.gloss: SHRM cross-industry CPH average ~$4,700
cards.verbatim: SHRM's cross-industry average is commonly cited at approximately $4,700[10].

cards.gloss: Percentile breakdown of CPH
cards.verbatim: One source's percentile breakdown gives a 25th percentile of $500, a median of $1,633, a 75th percentile of $4,669, and an average of $4,425[11]

cards.gloss: Median US CPH ~$1,633, executive CPH up to $28,000
cards.verbatim: another cites a median U.S. cost per hire of approximately $1,633 alongside executive-level hires reaching upwards of $28,000[12].

cards.gloss: 2026 guide: updated SHRM 2025 CPH average $5,475/$35,879, 21% increase since 2022
cards.verbatim: A 2026 guide states the $4,700 average is now outdated, citing SHRM's 2025 Benchmarking Report as putting the real U.S. average at $5,475 for non-executive roles and $35,879 for executive roles — a 21% increase from 2022[9].

cards.gloss: Another source's CPH figures: $4,683 non-executive, $28,329 executive
cards.verbatim: Another source gives $4,683 for non-executive roles and $28,329 for executive roles[7].

cards.gloss: Fully loaded employee cost reaches 1.25x-2.5x base salary
cards.verbatim: Separate from recruitment-specific cost metrics, the fully loaded cost of employing one person — including base salary, payroll taxes, health insurance contributions, retirement matching, workers' compensation, equipment, software licenses, and workspace — is estimated to routinely reach 1.25 to 2.5 times base salary[7].

cards.gloss: Itemized true-cost example for a $50,000 salary hire
cards.verbatim: For a $50,000 annual salary hire, the itemized estimate is: base salary $50,000; employer payroll taxes (FICA, FUTA, SUTA) approximately $4,500; health insurance employer contribution $6,000–$8,000; workers' compensation $500–$1,500; equipment $1,500–$3,000; software licenses/tools $500–$2,000; onboarding and training time cost $2,000–$4,000; for a total estimated first-year cost of $65,000–$74,000, or 1.3x to 1.48x base salary (reaching 2x or higher for roles with specialized equipment, higher benefits, or significant training needs)[7].

cards.gloss: Definition of direct/external costs
cards.verbatim: Direct costs — also referred to as external costs, since they represent money paid outward to third-party vendors rather than absorbed internally — are the most straightforward and quantifiable component of cost-per-hire (CPH), covering expenses that can be pointed to on a receipt and attached to one hire and one recruitment cycle[15].

cards.gloss: SHRM average CPH benchmark and its caveat
cards.verbatim: Benchmarks vary by source: SHRM places the average U.S. cost per hire at roughly $4,700 to $5,475, though this figure captures mostly direct costs and doesn't reveal whether it's good or bad without accounting for role mix, company size, and industry[15][16].

cards.gloss: Wider CPH range by role level, escalating with time-to-fill
cards.verbatim: Other industry research puts cost-per-hire in a wider range of $4,000–$20,000 depending on role level, with costs escalating the longer a position remains open[17].

cards.gloss: CPH scope boundary excludes post-hire costs
cards.verbatim: Notably, cost-per-hire is bounded at getting an employee to day one — it excludes post-hire costs like training beyond onboarding, productivity ramp-up, or ongoing employment costs, which belong to separate metrics like cost-of-vacancy and time-to-productivity[16][8].

cards.gloss: Job board/sourcing costs are a foundational direct expense
cards.verbatim: Job board and sourcing costs form a foundational direct expense.

cards.gloss: Job posting fee ranges (general, Indeed minimum, LinkedIn per-click)
cards.verbatim: Job posting fees run roughly $50–$500 per posting[18], though a single posting on Indeed has a minimum of around $150, and LinkedIn ads can charge roughly $5–9 per click[19].

cards.gloss: Monthly job ad spend in competitive/global hiring markets
cards.verbatim: In competitive markets, monthly job ad spend across multiple boards can run $500–$2,000 or more for a single role, and multinational firms hiring globally may spend more by localizing job boards or running social media campaigns in each region[19].

cards.gloss: Additional advertising cost categories (social media, print, careers page)
cards.verbatim: Costs also include social media advertising, print media, and career/careers page maintenance and updates (mobile optimization, current design)[20][21].

cards.gloss: Advertising cost pattern by role level
cards.verbatim: By role level: entry-level roles typically rely on broad job board postings and university career sites (lower cost); mid-level roles may need more targeted ads or professional network promotion; executive searches often skip public ads altogether, relying instead on specialized recruiters whose fee covers much of the "finding" work[19].

cards.gloss: Agency fees are one of the largest direct/external line items
cards.verbatim: Agency and third-party recruiter fees are consistently cited as one of the largest direct/external line items[19][18].

cards.gloss: Contingency search fee structure and rate range
cards.verbatim: **Contingency search** (common for mid-level roles): typically 15%–25% of the hire's first-year salary[15][19][8][18], with some niche or executive searches reaching up to 30%[19].

cards.gloss: Contingency search worked fee example
cards.verbatim: Example: a $70,000-salary role could carry a $10,500–$17,500 agency fee[19].

cards.gloss: Contingency search trade-off: volume over quality vetting
cards.verbatim: Contingency firms are paid only on placement, and because multiple firms often compete for the same placement, this model can favor volume over quality, with less thorough vetting and reduced access to passive candidates[22].

cards.gloss: Retained search fee structure and rate range
cards.verbatim: **Retained search** (standard for C-suite and senior executive roles): 25%–35% of total first-year compensation (base salary plus projected bonus)[19][22], sometimes reaching up to 40% for retained search generally[18], and up to 40%–50% of first-year income for C-level roles (CEO, CFO, CTO) at the top end[22].

cards.gloss: Retained search fee paid in three installments
cards.verbatim: Fees are typically paid in three installments: roughly one-third upon engagement, one-third when qualified candidates are presented, and the balance on placement[22].

cards.gloss: Retained search minimum and senior-executive fee amounts
cards.verbatim: Some firms set minimum fees between $80,000 and $100,000 depending on the position's salary, with fees for senior executives readily exceeding $150,000[22].

cards.gloss: Hybrid/retingency/container fee model
cards.verbatim: **Hybrid/"retingency"/container models**: a lesser upfront fee of 10%–25% of the total, with the remainder paid on placement — a middle ground best suited to director- and VP-level searches[22].

cards.gloss: Additional executive-search costs beyond the base fee
cards.verbatim: **Additional executive-search costs**: administrative fees of 10%–15%, plus travel, background checks, assessments, and marketing costs that can add another 5%–15% to the total engagement price[19][22].

cards.gloss: Agency fee comparison across role levels with dollar examples
cards.verbatim: By role level, entry-level hires carry the smallest absolute fees even at higher percentages (e.g., 20% of a $30,000 salary = $6,000), mid-level roles are "very often" filled via agencies at the 15%–25% rate, and executive hires can dwarf all other hiring costs — a 30% fee on a $200,000 executive salary equals $60,000[19].

cards.gloss: Geographic and industry variation in agency fees
cards.verbatim: Geographic and industry variation is significant: agencies in major metros (New York, San Francisco, Chicago) and in talent-scarce sectors (technology, financial, health sciences) command premium fees; in the UK, agencies commonly charge ~20% for general roles, but specialized searches can exceed £19,000 in fees[19][22].

cards.gloss: Background check cost ranges (basic vs comprehensive)
cards.verbatim: Basic background checks (criminal history, identity verification) run $30–$50[6], or $20–$50 per candidate in another estimate[19], while comprehensive packages (credit history, education/degree verification, employment history) cost $100–$150[6] to $100–$200[19].

cards.gloss: Drug testing cost range
cards.verbatim: Drug testing adds $30–$110 depending on the panel and whether it's lab-based[6].

cards.gloss: Screening costs multiply across the whole candidate pipeline, not just the hire
cards.verbatim: These costs multiply across every candidate screened in a pipeline for one role, not just the eventual hire[19].

cards.gloss: Pre-employment skills assessment cost range
cards.verbatim: Pre-employment skills assessments and testing tools cost $30 to $200 per candidate screened[16].

cards.gloss: Screening/assessment cost pattern by role level
cards.verbatim: By role level, entry-level hiring may involve more candidates and thus more (but cheaper per-candidate) checks; mid-level hires may use specialized assessments such as management aptitude tests that cost more per use; executive hiring involves the most extensive and priciest vetting (detailed background investigations, executive assessment services) despite a smaller candidate pool[19].

cards.gloss: Employee referral bonus range
cards.verbatim: Employee referral bonuses range from $500 to $5,000 per successful hire[16].

cards.gloss: Candidate travel/lodging/meal costs count toward CPH
cards.verbatim: Candidate travel and lodging expenses for out-of-town onsite interviews, along with meal stipends, count toward cost-per-hire[21].

cards.gloss: Relocation assistance cost range and delivery method
cards.verbatim: Relocation assistance, when applicable, can add $5,000 to $20,000+ per hire[16], delivered either as a lump sum after acceptance or as direct payment for moving, lodging, and travel costs, varying by seniority level[21].

cards.gloss: Career fair and event participation costs
cards.verbatim: Direct/external costs also include job fair and career-event participation: booth or presence fees, marketing materials (brochures, banners, promotional items), and recruiter travel, lodging, and meals for attending events[20][21].

cards.gloss: Employer branding spend and amortization treatment
cards.verbatim: Employer branding and sponsored content spend tied to recruiting is another external category[10][9], and when included, careers page and employer branding spend should be prorated annually and amortized across total hires[16].

cards.gloss: Recruitment technology/software cost and per-hire allocation
cards.verbatim: Recruitment technology and software — applicant tracking systems (ATS), video interview platforms, assessment tools — often carry subscription or licensing fees that factor into CPH, generally spread across all hires as HR overhead and amounting to a few hundred dollars per hire on average, though this adds up especially for smaller companies investing in enterprise-grade tools[23][19][21].

cards.gloss: Other miscellaneous external costs: legal fees and exit costs
cards.verbatim: Other cited external/miscellaneous items include legal fees for drafting employment contracts, and exit costs (severance, benefits continuation) when a hire is a replacement[20].

cards.gloss: Worked example of a small company's blended cost-per-hire calculation
cards.verbatim: One illustrative calculation: a 40-person company filling 8 roles in a quarter incurred $6,000 in external costs (job board posts, a couple of background checks, and one contingency agency fee) and $9,000 in internal costs (hiring manager and recruiter time), for a combined $15,000 ÷ 8 hires = $1,875 per hire — well below the SHRM average, which is expected given the company isn't filling executive or specialized technical roles at enterprise volume[9].

cards.gloss: Definition of indirect/soft costs as the largest, non-invoiced share of hiring cost
cards.verbatim: Indirect costs, often called soft costs, are the expenses of recruitment that never appear on an invoice yet typically make up the largest share of what a hire actually costs an organization[15].

cards.gloss: Indirect costs are harder to measure than direct costs
cards.verbatim: Unlike direct costs, which are easy to itemize, indirect costs are tied to time, productivity, and risk, and are therefore harder to measure and easy to underestimate[15].

cards.gloss: Indirect costs estimated at 60-70% of total hiring cost
cards.verbatim: Industry estimates place indirect costs at roughly 60-70% of the true total cost of hiring[6],

cards.gloss: Indirect costs estimated at 3-10x direct costs for a bad hire
cards.verbatim: while other analyses put them at 3-10 times larger than direct costs specifically in the context of a bad hire[24].

cards.gloss: SHRM's $5,475 cost-per-hire figure only captures direct costs; real total 2-3x higher
cards.verbatim: SHRM's widely cited average cost-per-hire figure of about $5,475 (elsewhere cited as roughly $4,700-$5,475) captures mostly direct costs; once indirect costs are added, the real total often runs two to three times higher[15].

cards.gloss: Internal staff time spent on hiring tasks is a major indirect cost source
cards.verbatim: A substantial share of indirect cost comes from the hours internal staff spend on the hiring process rather than revenue-generating work: writing job descriptions, reviewing resumes, conducting interviews, and scoring candidates[15][19].

cards.gloss: In-house TA specialist salary works out to ~$2,000 per hire
cards.verbatim: If an in-house Talent Acquisition specialist earns $60,000-$80,000 per year and handles approximately 40 hires annually, that works out to roughly $2,000 per hire in salary cost alone, before counting the time of hiring managers and interview panel members[19].

cards.gloss: Extra interview rounds multiply time cost across panel members
cards.verbatim: Each additional interview round multiplies this further, since panels typically involve two or more managers or team members whose time must also be costed in[19].

cards.gloss: Small businesses without HR see indirect costs exceed direct costs
cards.verbatim: For small businesses without a dedicated HR function, this burden falls disproportionately on the founder or manager, whose time is often the most expensive resource in the company; as a result, indirect costs for small businesses typically exceed direct costs[25].

cards.gloss: Unfilled roles carry a direct productivity cost
cards.verbatim: Unfilled roles carry a direct productivity cost.

cards.gloss: SHRM 2020 study: monthly cost of a vacant position
cards.verbatim: A 2020 SHRM study found the average cost of a vacant position ranges from $4,129 to $5,733 per month, depending on industry and role, and can run significantly higher for high-demand positions in technology or healthcare[26].

cards.gloss: Vacancy productivity loss estimate of ~$100/day
cards.verbatim: One estimate puts vacancy productivity loss at roughly $100 per day a role sits open[6].

cards.gloss: Average time to fill has risen from 29 to 43 days since 2010
cards.verbatim: Compounding this, the average time to fill a U.S. position has risen to 43 days, up from 29 days in 2010, according to LinkUp[26] — meaning the vacancy-cost window has grown substantially over the past decade.

cards.gloss: Vacancy period effects: overtime burden, morale, productivity, lost customers
cards.verbatim: During this period, existing employees often absorb the missing workload through overtime, and organizations can face decreased morale, reduced productivity, and even lost clients or customers due to diminished service levels[26][15].

cards.gloss: Onboarding indirect costs after offer acceptance
cards.verbatim: Once a candidate accepts an offer, indirect costs continue through onboarding: HR and manager time spent on orientation, onboarding software or materials, and sometimes travel, lodging, or a welcome package for the new hire[19].

cards.gloss: Average U.S. onboarding cost benchmark
cards.verbatim: Benchmarks put average U.S. onboarding cost at roughly $1,500-$5,000 per employee[19].

cards.gloss: Training has both direct and indirect (lost productivity) costs
cards.verbatim: Training carries both direct costs (course fees, trainer salaries, e-learning subscriptions) and indirect costs, since a new hire in training is not yet fully productive[23][19].

cards.gloss: Productivity gap persists through ramp-up period
cards.verbatim: This productivity gap persists through the ramp-up period, as the new employee builds toward full effectiveness[6][15].

cards.gloss: Administrative processing costs tied to each new hire
cards.verbatim: Indirect costs also include administrative processing tied to each new hire: payroll setup, benefits enrollment, equipment provisioning, and records work[15][27].

cards.gloss: Employee benefits should be factored into hiring-cost assessment
cards.verbatim: Employee benefits associated with new hires — health insurance, retirement contributions, and other perks — vary by the organization's compensation structure but should be factored into any comprehensive hiring-cost assessment[23].

cards.gloss: A mis-hire is the most expensive indirect cost
cards.verbatim: The most expensive indirect cost is a mis-hire.

cards.gloss: Gallup: replacing an employee costs 50-200% of annual salary
cards.verbatim: Gallup estimates that replacing an employee costs 50% to 200% of their annual salary[6][15][25].

cards.gloss: Concrete replacement cost examples for entry-level vs senior roles
cards.verbatim: Applied concretely: a $50,000 entry-level position carries roughly $25,000 in replacement costs, while a $100,000 senior role can run $200,000 or more[6].

cards.gloss: Replacement cost figures include rehiring plus vacancy/ramp-up productivity losses
cards.verbatim: These figures capture the full cost of rehiring plus productivity losses during the vacancy and the ramp-up of the replacement[6].

cards.gloss: Bad-hire indirect costs beyond replacement search, 3-10x direct costs
cards.verbatim: Beyond the replacement search itself, a bad hire generates indirect costs including lost leadership time, team productivity drag, missed performance targets, delayed projects, and negative cultural impact — costs that are typically 3-10 times larger than the direct costs of hiring[24].

cards.gloss: Decision guidance: when cost of waiting on a struggling hire exceeds restarting the search
cards.verbatim: Decision guidance on this point: if role clarity and performance expectations were clear from the start and a performance gap persists after 60-90 days of focused support, the cost of continuing to wait on a struggling hire typically exceeds the cost of restarting the search[24].

cards.gloss: Organizations tracking only invoiced spend miss the larger indirect-cost half
cards.verbatim: Because hard costs are visible on a ledger and soft costs are diffused across many people's time, organizations that track only invoiced spending are managing the smaller half of their hiring budget while flying blind on the larger half[15].

cards.gloss: Comprehensive cost-per-hire formula sums external and internal costs
cards.verbatim: The comprehensive cost-per-hire formula accounts for this by summing both categories: Total Cost-Per-Hire = (External Costs + Internal Costs) ÷ Number of Hires[27],

cards.gloss: Components that make up internal costs in the formula
cards.verbatim: with internal costs comprising internal HR time, hiring manager time, team interview time, onboarding and training hours, reduced productivity during the transition, and administrative processing time[27].

cards.gloss: Vacancy costs go beyond salary
cards.verbatim: Vacancy costs extend well past the salary line item.

cards.gloss: Recruitment marketing spend and background burnout/retention risk during a vacancy
cards.verbatim: Money spent on job boards and other recruitment marketing platforms accumulates during the search, while team burnout and possible employee retention issues build in the background[28].

cards.gloss: Hidden vacancy effects compound past tracked costs
cards.verbatim: Lower productivity, missed deadlines, and decreased customer satisfaction round out the standard list of hidden vacancy effects, and these compound quickly, often exceeding the direct vacancy costs organizations actually track[28].

cards.gloss: Hidden costs vary by industry/role (engineering, manufacturing, construction)
cards.verbatim: Hidden vacancy cost variables also shift by industry and role: technical roles in engineering and manufacturing carry hidden costs like stalled product launches and disrupted production timelines the longer they stay open, while construction-related roles carry their own analogous delays[28].

cards.gloss: 38% of SMBs underestimate hiring costs due to ANSI formula gaps
cards.verbatim: Industry-wide, 38% of small and mid-size businesses underestimate their hiring costs, according to research compiled by Truffle, because the ANSI cost-per-hire formula excludes these hidden expenses even though they drive real budget decisions every quarter[18].

cards.gloss: Interview time pulls hiring managers/staff from their primary work
cards.verbatim: When hiring managers and team members conduct interviews, they are not accomplishing their primary responsibilities, which can lead to delayed projects and missed deadlines that show up in reduced product output and profitability[21].

cards.gloss: Broader vacancy productivity loss is harder to measure than internal-time cost
cards.verbatim: This internal-time cost can be calculated, but the broader productivity loss from a vacancy is harder to measure and is frequently the piece left out of formal cost-per-hire calculations even though it represents a real opportunity cost[23][21].

cards.gloss: Gallup: overtime-driven burnout can cut productivity up to 68%
cards.verbatim: Gallup reports that overtime-driven burnout can cut productivity by up to 68%

cards.gloss: Burned-out employees are 2.6x more likely to leave
cards.verbatim: burned-out employees are 2.6 times more likely to leave[26]

cards.gloss: Vacancy duration creates a self-reinforcing double-duty/turnover cycle
cards.verbatim: The longer a role stays vacant, the longer employees work double duty, putting the company at risk of worsening engagement that can itself result in turnover — a self-reinforcing cycle in which an unfilled role generates the conditions for the next one[21].

cards.gloss: 85% of hiring pros say a bad hire hurts the whole team (LinkedIn survey)
cards.verbatim: For bad hires specifically, a LinkedIn survey found that 85% of hiring professionals reported that a bad hire negatively affected the entire team, not just the company's balance sheet[29].

cards.gloss: 33% of customers would switch providers after one poor service experience (Amex)
cards.verbatim: Understaffing degrades service quality: one poor service experience prompts 33% of customers to consider switching providers, according to an American Express survey[26].

cards.gloss: Forrester: 1-point CSAT lift equals roughly $1B revenue for a Fortune 1000 firm
cards.verbatim: The upside case is equally sharp — Forrester finds that even a 1-point lift in customer satisfaction can translate to roughly $1 billion in revenue for a typical Fortune 1000 firm, illustrating the scale of what prolonged vacancies or poor hires put at risk[26].

cards.gloss: HBR: 80% of customer service issues stem from employee-related challenges
cards.verbatim: Harvard Business Review research suggests that 80% of customer service issues stem from employee-related challenges, reinforcing that hiring quality has a direct line to reputation and retention[31].

cards.gloss: New hires ramp up slowly, causing short-term support/error-rate issues
cards.verbatim: New employees also take longer to complete their work and are typically less skilled at resolving problems in their early period, which creates a short-term customer support and error-rate challenge[32].

cards.gloss: Managing a performance gap costs leadership 10-15 hours/week
cards.verbatim: Management time drain is largely invisible on spreadsheets but deeply felt: leadership time spent managing a performance gap typically runs 10–15 hours per week

cards.gloss: Surrounding team productivity drops 15-25% during a performance-gap situation
cards.verbatim: the surrounding team's productivity typically declines 15–25% while the situation persists[24][29]

cards.gloss: Bad-hire indirect costs run 3-10x the direct spreadsheet costs
cards.verbatim: For a bad hire, indirect costs — lost leadership time, team productivity drag, missed performance, delayed projects, and negative cultural impact — are typically 3–10 times larger than the direct costs that show up on a spreadsheet (salary, benefits, recruiting fees, training)[24].

cards.gloss: Average US company training spend ~$1,300/employee/year, higher for technical roles
cards.verbatim: The average U.S. company spends approximately $1,300 per employee per year on training, according to the Association for Talent Development, and this figure runs several times higher for specialized or technical roles[29].

cards.gloss: 2024 training cost ~$874/employee; 20 hires can exceed $17,000/year
cards.verbatim: Separately, workforce data puts the cost of training one U.S. employee in 2024 at $874 a year; a company hiring 20 workers in a rapid-growth period can see annual training costs exceed $17,000[32].

cards.gloss: Cost of a bad hiring mistake has grown over time from roughly $15,000
cards.verbatim: The scale of what counts as an expensive hiring mistake has grown over time: what was a $15,000 mistake a few years ago can now spiral into tens of thousands more if left unchecked, reflecting a broader trend of rising financial penalties for rushed, instinct-based, or misaligned hiring[29].

cards.gloss: Gallup: disengaged employees cost $3,400 per $10,000 in salary
cards.verbatim: A Gallup study found that disengaged employees cost businesses $3,400 for every $10,000 in salary through lost productivity alone, a ratio that scales directly with the size and pay level of the disengaged group[29].

cards.gloss: Recruitment cost varies by seniority, complexity, skill rarity, industry, and geography
cards.verbatim: Recruitment cost is not a flat number: it moves sharply with the seniority, complexity, and rarity of the skills required for a given role, and with the industry and geography the search takes place in[33].

cards.gloss: C-suite roles draw elevated fees due to more extensive search/vetting
cards.verbatim: Higher-level and C-suite positions consistently draw elevated search fees because they demand a more extensive search and vetting process

cards.gloss: Rarer required skill sets push fees higher
cards.verbatim: the rarer the required skill set, the higher the fee tends to run[33].

cards.gloss: Talent-scarce industries like tech see higher fees across the board
cards.verbatim: Competitive, talent-scarce industries such as technology see higher recruitment fees across the board

cards.gloss: Searches in major metro areas cost more due to higher operating costs
cards.verbatim: searches based in major metropolitan areas cost more due to the higher cost of operating there[33].

cards.gloss: CPH data source: Bersin by Deloitte and LinkedIn Talent Solutions
cards.verbatim: Average cost-per-hire (CPH) data compiled from sources including Bersin by Deloitte and LinkedIn's Talent Solutions annual reports shows a wide spread by role type[7]:

cards.gloss: CPH for general/non-executive roles
cards.verbatim: | General / Non-executive | ~$4,683 |

cards.gloss: CPH for executive/senior leadership roles
cards.verbatim: | Executive / Senior Leadership | ~$28,329 |

cards.gloss: CPH for tech/engineering roles
cards.verbatim: | Tech / Engineering | $6,000 – $10,000+ |

cards.gloss: CPH for hourly/entry-level roles
cards.verbatim: | Hourly / Entry-Level | $1,000 – $2,500 |

cards.gloss: CPH for healthcare clinical roles
cards.verbatim: | Healthcare (clinical roles) | $5,000 – $9,000 |

cards.gloss: CPH for manufacturing skilled trades roles
cards.verbatim: | Manufacturing (skilled trades) | $3,500 – $7,000 |

cards.gloss: SHRM 2024 baseline CPH of $4,700, up 14% from pre-pandemic, vs $28,329 executive average
cards.verbatim: SHRM's own benchmark for a standard hire puts baseline cost-per-hire at $4,700 in 2024, a 14% increase over pre-pandemic levels, against an executive-level average of $28,329[29].

cards.gloss: Gap between general and executive CPH reflects sourcing complexity, stakeholder involvement, external search firm reliance
cards.verbatim: That gap reflects the difference in sourcing complexity, stakeholder involvement, and reliance on external search firms at the senior end[7].

cards.gloss: Example: 50 warehouse hires at $1,500 each totals $75,000 quarterly
cards.verbatim: hiring 50 warehouse associates in a quarter at $1,500 each represents $75,000 in quarterly spend

cards.gloss: High-volume hiring needs a different cost-management approach than executive search
cards.verbatim: high-volume hiring requires a different cost-management approach than low-volume executive search[7].

cards.gloss: Agency/search-firm fees scale with role level as a percent of first-year salary
cards.verbatim: Recruitment agency and search-firm fees scale directly with role level, typically expressed as a percentage of first-year salary[33][19]:

cards.gloss: Entry-level agency fees run around 20% of salary
cards.verbatim: many organizations avoid agencies here to save money, but where used, fees run around 20% of salary

cards.gloss: Entry-level fee example: $30,000 role costs ~$6,000 in fees
cards.verbatim: on a $30,000 role, roughly $6,000 in absolute terms, still a meaningful percentage despite the low dollar figure[19].

cards.gloss: Mid-level fees run 15-25% via agencies/headhunters
cards.verbatim: filled via agencies or headhunters more often, with fees in the 15–25% range[19].

cards.gloss: Board director/top-exec placements have highest fee %; mid-level executive placements lower
cards.verbatim: Board director and top-executive placements sit at the high end of the fee spectrum, while mid-level executive placements typically command lower percentage fees by comparison[22].

cards.gloss: External recruiters used almost universally for senior hires, at high cost
cards.verbatim: external recruiters are used almost universally for senior hires, at a high cost.

cards.gloss: Example: $200k executive salary at 30% fee = $60,000 recruiting fee
cards.verbatim: A $200,000 executive salary at a 30% fee produces a $60,000 recruiting fee alone, which can dwarf every other hiring cost combined[19].

cards.gloss: Executive search fees broadly range 25-35% of first-year compensation, aligning firm incentives
cards.verbatim: Executive search fees more broadly range from 25% to 35% of the candidate's first-year compensation, a model that aligns the search firm's incentives with finding the best possible candidate[33].

cards.gloss: Example: CMO search at $200k base generates $40k-$60k placement fee
cards.verbatim: an executive search firm engaged to fill a Chief Marketing Officer role at $200,000 base salary generates a placement fee of $40,000 to $60,000 before internal costs are even counted[7].

cards.gloss: Senior roles can cost 3-4x salary to fill once all costs included
cards.verbatim: Many employers report senior roles can cost three to four times salary to fill once all cost components are included[19].

cards.gloss: Flat-fee model: fixed cost for entire executive search, need to confirm coverage
cards.verbatim: Flat-fee models offer an alternative at the executive level, charging several thousand to tens of thousands of dollars for the entire search, useful for organizations with a defined scope and budget, though buyers need to confirm exactly what the flat fee covers to avoid unexpected add-ons[33].

cards.gloss: Hybrid fee model: upfront payment plus placement-contingent remainder
cards.verbatim: Hybrid models require an initial payment upfront with the remainder contingent on placement

cards.gloss: Pure contingency model ties full fee to successful placement
cards.verbatim: pure contingency models tie the full fee to successful placement[33].

cards.gloss: Difference between 25% contingency and 33% retained fee is negligible vs cost of a bad hire
cards.verbatim: Against the cost of a failed search, the choice between fee structures matters less than it appears: the difference between a 25% contingency fee and a 33% retained search fee is described as negligible when weighed against the price of a bad hire[22].

cards.gloss: SHRM replacement-cost range of 50-200% of annual salary, from Human Capital Benchmarking Reports
cards.verbatim: SHRM's widely cited replacement-cost range of 50% to 200% of annual salary, drawn from its Human Capital Benchmarking Reports

cards.gloss: Replacement cost breakdown by seniority: entry 50-75%, mid 100-150%, C-suite 200%+
cards.verbatim: entry-level roles trend toward 50–75%, mid-level managerial and technical roles toward 100–150%, and C-suite or executive positions toward 200% or above[29].

cards.gloss: Failed executive hire can cost 3-5x annual salary including productivity/morale/strategic loss
cards.verbatim: At the extreme end, a failed executive hire can set an organization back 3–5 times the executive's annual salary once lost productivity, morale damage, and foregone strategic opportunity are factored in[29][22].

cards.gloss: Bad management-level hire costs $300,000-$500,000 in total organizational cost
cards.verbatim: A bad hire at the management level specifically has been put at $300,000 to $500,000 in total organizational cost[24].

cards.gloss: Mid-level bad hires cost 1-3x annual salary in replacement cost
cards.verbatim: Mid-level bad hires carry a replacement cost of one to three times annual salary once recruitment fees, onboarding, and early attrition are included

cards.gloss: Lower mid-level bad-hire cost makes overlooked internal candidates lower risk than failed external senior hires
cards.verbatim: an asymmetry that makes overlooked internal candidates comparatively low-risk against a failed external senior hire[29].

cards.gloss: 74% of employers admit to hiring the wrong person (CareerBuilder)
cards.verbatim: CareerBuilder research found 74% of employers admitted to hiring the wrong person for a role

cards.gloss: Average direct loss of $14,900-$17,000 per poor hiring decision
cards.verbatim: with average direct losses of $14,900 to $17,000 per poor hiring decision[29].

cards.gloss: Managers spent 17% of workweek in 2024 correcting poorly performing hires' mistakes
cards.verbatim: managers spent an average of 17% of their workweek in 2024 supervising, documenting, and correcting the mistakes of poorly performing hires

cards.gloss: Time-to-fill lengthens with seniority
cards.verbatim: Time-to-fill lengthens as seniority rises[3]:

cards.gloss: Senior-level roles: ~40% take 90+ days to fill
cards.verbatim: Senior-level roles: nearly 40% take more than 90 days to fill.

cards.gloss: Mid-level roles: 44% take 31-60 days, 17% exceed 90 days
cards.verbatim: Mid-level roles: 44% fall in the 31–60 day window, while 17% stretch past 90 days.

cards.gloss: Exempt roles: 44% take 31-60 days, ~40% exceed 90 days
cards.verbatim: Exempt roles overall: 44% fall in 31–60 days, but almost 40% push past 90.

cards.gloss: Nonexempt roles: most fill in 30-60 days, 25% exceed 90 days
cards.verbatim: Nonexempt roles: most fill in 30–60 days, though 25% extend beyond 90.

cards.gloss: Across all roles, a quarter of searches take 90+ days
cards.verbatim: Across roles generally, a quarter of searches report 90+ days.

cards.gloss: Specialized/niche roles take 2-3x longer to fill, multiplying cost
cards.verbatim: Specialized or niche roles requiring rare skills or extensive certifications often take two to three times longer to fill than standard roles, which multiplies every associated cost[17].

cards.gloss: Extended C-suite vacancies create strategic uncertainty, affect investor confidence and board dynamics
cards.verbatim: Extended C-suite vacancies carry consequences beyond time: they create strategic uncertainty and can affect investor confidence and board dynamics[17].

cards.gloss: Vacancy cost is driven by role's revenue/operational function, not just seniority
cards.verbatim: Seniority is not the only driver of vacancy cost; the revenue or operational role a position plays matters just as much[17].

cards.gloss: Vacancy cost modeling method: revenue per employee per day times days vacant
cards.verbatim: vacancy cost can be modeled as average revenue per employee per day multiplied by days vacant

cards.gloss: Example: sales rep generating $500k/yr, 90-day vacancy costs ~$180,000 in lost revenue
cards.verbatim: a sales representative generating $500,000 annually produces roughly $2,000 per working day, so a 90-day vacancy costs approximately $180,000 in lost revenue opportunity[17].

cards.gloss: Executive vacancies carry hard-to-quantify but materially significant strategic uncertainty costs
cards.verbatim: Executive positions carry strategic uncertainty costs that are harder to quantify but are flagged as materially significant

cards.gloss: Specialized/niche roles multiply vacancy cost via longer fill times
cards.verbatim: specialized or niche roles multiply cost through longer fill times

cards.gloss: High-volume roles produce large aggregate vacancy cost despite low per-vacancy impact
cards.verbatim: high-volume roles produce substantial aggregate vacancy cost even though each individual vacancy has lower impact[17].

cards.gloss: SHRM: every open position costs $4,000-$9,000/month in lost productivity, overtime, burnout
cards.verbatim: SHRM data separately estimates every open position costs an organization between $4,000 and $9,000 per month in lost productivity, overtime, and burnout

cards.gloss: This monthly vacancy cost multiplies for long-vacant mid-level/executive roles
cards.verbatim: a figure that multiplies when mid-level or executive roles stay vacant for months at a time[3][26].

cards.gloss: CPH varies by industry due to skills, credentialing, scarcity, and competition
cards.verbatim: it varies sharply by industry, driven by differences in required skills, credentialing burdens, talent scarcity, and competitive intensity [18]

cards.gloss: Benchmark CPH ranges by industry: healthcare, skilled trades, legal/professional services
cards.verbatim: healthcare roles run $9,000-$12,000 per hire, skilled trades positions cost $12,000 or more, and legal/professional services hires run $16,000-$20,000 [18]

cards.gloss: Healthcare is the most expensive category, running 2-3x the national average
cards.verbatim: Healthcare stands out as the most expensive category — between credential verification, licensing requirements, and an ongoing talent shortage, healthcare organizations routinely spend two to three times the national average per hire [18]

cards.gloss: Alternate benchmark: healthcare ~$5,000 vs hospitality $2,700, showing figures diverge by methodology/source
cards.verbatim: A separate benchmark set puts healthcare CPH at roughly $5,000, compared with just $2,700 for a new hire in the hospitality industry, underscoring that even within "high-cost" classifications the reported figures diverge depending on methodology and source [21]

cards.gloss: Drivers of higher healthcare recruiting costs: credential verification, licensing, staffing agencies
cards.verbatim: credential verification, licensing checks, and reliance on specialized healthcare staffing agencies push costs higher

cards.gloss: RN and physician recruiter fees often exceed 20% of first-year compensation
cards.verbatim: registered nurse and physician recruiter fees often exceed 20% of first-year compensation [7]

cards.gloss: Tech/software roles carry a premium due to competition in major tech markets
cards.verbatim: Technology and software development roles carry their own premium: competition for engineering and software talent in markets such as San Francisco, Austin, Seattle, and New York drives up sourcing costs, assessment complexity, and time-to-fill [7]

cards.gloss: Manufacturing CPH moderate but rising in 2025 due to Midwest/Southeast shortages
cards.verbatim: Manufacturing organizations see moderate CPH ranges for skilled-trades positions, but geographic concentration and skilled-labor shortages in the US Midwest and Southeast are pushing those figures upward in 2025 [7]

cards.gloss: Executive search fees are premium in tech, financial services, health sciences; lower in less technical industries
cards.verbatim: Technology, financial services, and health sciences industries — which typically experience shortages of skilled professionals — command premium executive search fees, while less technically driven industries see reduced fee levels [22]

cards.gloss: C-level executive search fees can reach 40-50% of first-year income
cards.verbatim: C-level roles (CEO, CFO, CTO) can command fees at the top end ranging from 40-50% of first-year income [22]

cards.gloss: Larger organizations report lower CPH due to more resources and faster fill times
cards.verbatim: Larger organizations typically report lower cost-per-hire figures because they have more resources, more efficient recruitment processes, and can fill roles as much as five days faster than small-to-mid-sized counterparts [21]

cards.gloss: Smaller business units have higher CPH due to fewer hires and limited recruitment budget
cards.verbatim: Smaller business units make fewer hires and often lack the budget for an extensive recruitment strategy, which makes their cost-per-hire comparatively more expensive [18][21]

cards.gloss: Survey: CPH is the top HR metric for small businesses since each hire carries more budget weight
cards.verbatim: CPH is the number one HR metric for 47% of businesses with 5-19 employees and 54% of businesses with 20-49 employees, since with only 5-10 hires per year (versus 500 for an enterprise), each hiring decision carries disproportionate weight on the budget [18]

cards.gloss: Enterprises spread fixed recruiting costs across many hires, lowering per-hire figure
cards.verbatim: Enterprise organizations, by contrast, spread fixed costs — ATS licenses, recruiter salaries, employer branding — across hundreds or thousands of hires annually, lowering the per-hire figure [18]

cards.gloss: 1.25x-2.5x rule of thumb for small businesses to estimate true cost of a hire
cards.verbatim: For small businesses without a dedicated talent acquisition function, a 1.25x to 2.5x rule of thumb is offered as a faster way to estimate the real cost of a hire [7]

cards.gloss: Major-city HQ gives access to larger talent pool but higher cost-of-living pushes up salaries/benefits
cards.verbatim: companies headquartered in major cities have access to a larger talent pool but also face higher cost-of-living pressures that push up required salaries and benefits

cards.gloss: Executive search fees are higher in large markets (NY, SF, Chicago) than smaller markets
cards.verbatim: firms in large markets like New York, San Francisco, and Chicago are generally more costly than those in smaller markets

cards.gloss: Global executive searches command premium fees due to added complexity
cards.verbatim: global searches, being more complex, command premium fees on top of that [22]

cards.gloss: Company size counterintuitively drives cost-per-hire: smaller companies pay more per hire despite spending less overall
cards.verbatim: Company size is one of the largest drivers of cost-per-hire variation, and the direction is counterintuitive: smaller companies routinely pay more per hire than large enterprises, despite spending less in total.[18]

cards.gloss: Large enterprises spread fixed recruiting costs across many hires and run streamlined, dedicated HR teams
cards.verbatim: Large enterprises benefit from scale. They spread fixed recruiting costs (ATS licenses, recruiter salaries, employer branding) across hundreds or thousands of hires per year, and often maintain dedicated HR teams with streamlined, repeatable processes that reduce the cost of any single hire.[18][10]

cards.gloss: Illustration: $200k/2-recruiter team vs $2M/20-recruiter,1000-hire enterprise — smaller total spend but worse per-hire math
cards.verbatim: A useful illustration: a company spending $200,000 on a two-person recruiting team will have a much higher per-hire cost than an enterprise spreading $2 million across 20 recruiters making 1,000 hires — the total spend is smaller, but the per-hire math is worse.[18]

cards.gloss: SMBs lack scale: no dedicated recruiting teams, rely on agencies/job boards, lack brand recognition, need extra ad/outreach spend
cards.verbatim: Small and mid-size businesses lack this scale. They don't have dedicated recruiting teams, rely more heavily on agencies or job board postings, and often lack the brand recognition needed to attract candidates quickly — forcing additional investment in advertising or outreach.[18][10]

cards.gloss: Fewer annual hires (5-10 vs 500) means each hire carries disproportionate budget weight since fixed costs can't be amortized
cards.verbatim: When a business makes 5-10 hires per year instead of 500, each individual hiring decision carries disproportionate weight on the budget, since fixed costs can't be amortized the way an enterprise can.[18]

cards.gloss: Small/mid-size teams are almost certainly above the $5,475 average cost-per-hire; being above average is framed as normal, proportional quality is what matters
cards.verbatim: The result: small and mid-size teams are almost certainly above the $5,475 average cost-per-hire figure, and this is described as normal — whether a business is above average matters less than whether it's getting proportional quality for that spending.[18]

cards.gloss: Cost-per-hire is the #1 tracked HR metric for 47% of businesses with 5-19 employees and 54% of businesses with 20-49 employees
cards.verbatim: Cost-per-hire is reported as the number one HR metric tracked by 47% of businesses with 5-19 employees and 54% of businesses with 20-49 employees, reflecting how much weight smaller organizations place on this figure given their tighter margins.[18]

cards.gloss: One source: real small-business hiring cost is $5,500-$24,000/hire vs. the SHRM $4,700 average, which it calls misleading for SMBs
cards.verbatim: One source puts the real cost of hiring a new employee for a small business at $5,500-$24,000 per hire, compared with the oft-cited SHRM average of $4,700 — a figure the source calls "misleading" for small businesses because it blends in huge enterprises with dedicated recruiting teams, bulk discounts, and economies of scale that small businesses don't have.[6]

cards.gloss: By this account, small businesses pay about 53% more per hire than enterprises
cards.verbatim: By this account, small businesses pay about 53% more per hire than enterprises.[6]

cards.gloss: Concrete example: 10-person company hiring at $50k salary — low estimate is a quick network/single-posting hire, high estimate is a harder multi-round search with external recruiters
cards.verbatim: For a concrete example: a 10-person company hiring one new employee at a $50,000 salary sees a wide range depending on circumstances — the low estimate assumes a quick hire through network or a single job posting with fast ramp-up, while the high estimate reflects a harder search, multiple interview rounds, external recruiters, and a longer time to productivity, with most hires falling somewhere in between.[6]

cards.gloss: SMBs typically don't pay for an ATS, which costs enterprises $100-$500/month
cards.verbatim: They typically do not pay for an ATS, which costs enterprises $100-$500/month.[25]

cards.gloss: SMBs rarely use agencies for standard roles, which cost enterprises $9,000-$15,000 per placement
cards.verbatim: They rarely use agencies for standard roles, which cost enterprises $9,000-$15,000 per placement.[25]

cards.gloss: SMBs have zero recruiting staff overhead — no recruiter salary, TA coordinator, or employer branding team
cards.verbatim: They have zero recruiting staff overhead — no recruiter salary, no talent-acquisition coordinator, no employer branding team.[25]

cards.gloss: Trade-off: money saved on recruiting tools/staff is replaced by founder time, which is harder to quantify but equally costly
cards.verbatim: The trade-off is that every dollar saved on tools and staff is replaced by founder time, which is harder to quantify but equally expensive.[25]

cards.gloss: Entry-level SMB hire costs: $500-$1,200 direct / $2,000-$4,000 total; high supply, low screening complexity, fast hire
cards.verbatim: | Entry-level (admin, customer service, retail) | $500-$1,200 | $2,000-$4,000 | High supply, low screening complexity, fast hire |

cards.gloss: Mid-level SMB hire costs: $1,000-$2,500 direct / $3,500-$7,000 total; moderate screening, may need skills testing
cards.verbatim: | Mid-level (operations, marketing, bookkeeping) | $1,000-$2,500 | $3,500-$7,000 | Moderate screening, may require skills testing |

cards.gloss: Senior/specialized SMB hire costs: $2,000-$5,000 direct / $6,000-$12,000 total; limited supply, longer search, may need agency
cards.verbatim: | Senior/specialized (developer, controller, manager) | $2,000-$5,000 | $6,000-$12,000 | Limited supply, longer search, may need agency |

cards.gloss: Executive SMB hire costs: $5,000-$15,000+ direct / $15,000-$40,000+ total; agency/retained search typical, extended timeline
cards.verbatim: | Executive (VP, director, C-suite) | $5,000-$15,000+ | $15,000-$40,000+ | Agency or retained search typical, extended timeline |

cards.gloss: Roughly 80% of small-business hires fall into the entry-level and mid-level categories
cards.verbatim: For most small businesses, roughly 80% of hires fall into the entry-level and mid-level categories.[25]

cards.gloss: Healthcare orgs spend 2-3x the national average per hire due to credentialing, licensing, and talent shortage, compounding the size-driven gap
cards.verbatim: Industry-specific cost pressure can compound the company-size effect: healthcare organizations, for instance, routinely spend two to three times the national average per hire due to credential verification, licensing requirements, and an ongoing talent shortage — a pattern that compounds rather than replaces the size-driven gap.[18]

cards.gloss: Recruitment costs vary by geography, industry, company size, and role level, with compounding factors
cards.verbatim: Recruitment costs are not uniform across geography, industry, company size, or role level, and multiple factors compound to determine where an organization sits relative to national benchmarks.

cards.gloss: CPH varies by industry due to hiring practices, talent availability, competition
cards.verbatim: Cost-per-hire (CPH) varies significantly by industry because different sectors face different hiring practices, talent availability, and competition for skilled workers[23].

cards.gloss: Tech and healthcare sectors face higher CPH due to specialized skills
cards.verbatim: Technology and healthcare sectors face higher CPH due to the specialized skills required and the competitive nature of talent acquisition[23].

cards.gloss: Geographic location and cost of living drive up hiring costs via competitive salaries
cards.verbatim: the geographic location of an organization plays a crucial role in determining CPH, since regions with a higher cost of living require more competitive salaries and benefits, driving up hiring costs[23].

cards.gloss: 2025 engineering/software talent demand in major tech hubs raises sourcing costs and time-to-fill
cards.verbatim: In 2025, high demand for engineering and software development talent in markets such as San Francisco, Austin, Seattle, and New York drives up sourcing costs, assessment complexity, and time-to-fill[7].

cards.gloss: Healthcare employers face elevated CPH from credentialing, licensing, and staffing agency reliance
cards.verbatim: Healthcare employers face elevated CPH for clinical and licensed roles because of credential verification requirements, licensing checks, and reliance on specialized healthcare staffing agencies

cards.gloss: RN and physician recruiter fees often exceed 20% of first-year compensation
cards.verbatim: registered nurse and physician recruiter fees often exceed 20% of first-year compensation[7].

cards.gloss: Manufacturing sees moderate CPH but Midwest/Southeast skilled-labor shortages pushing figures up in 2025
cards.verbatim: Manufacturing organizations see moderate CPH ranges for skilled trades positions, but geographic concentration and skilled labor shortages in the US Midwest and Southeast are pushing those figures upward in 2025[7].

cards.gloss: Geography interacts with company size/hiring volume to shift expected CPH (startup vs enterprise example)
cards.verbatim: Geography interacts with company size and hiring volume to shift expected CPH: a 10-person startup in a secondary market fills roles at a different cost profile than a 5,000-person enterprise in a major metro area[7].

cards.verbatim: Benchmark data by company size shows small businesses under 100 employees typically see $3,500 to $5,500 per hire

cards.gloss: Mid-market companies (100-999 employees) CPH benchmark: $2,500-$4,500
cards.verbatim: mid-market companies with 100-999 employees range from $2,500 to $4,500

cards.verbatim: enterprise organizations with 1,000+ employees often achieve $1,500 to $3,500 per hire[16].

cards.verbatim: Enterprise cost per hire tends to be lower due to economies of scale in recruiting infrastructure, higher hiring volume spreading fixed costs across more hires, and stronger employer brand reducing paid-sourcing dependency[16].

cards.gloss: SHRM benchmark: average US cost per hire is approximately $4,700
cards.verbatim: The SHRM benchmark places the average US cost per hire at approximately $4,700[16]

cards.verbatim: SHRM's 2025 Benchmarking Survey (fielded January 9 to March 3, 2025, with 2,371 member respondents) reports nonexecutive average CPH of $5,475 versus executive average CPH of $35,879

cards.gloss: Executive hires run nearly 7x more expensive than nonexecutive hires
cards.verbatim: executive hires run nearly 7x more expensive than nonexecutive hires[34][16].

cards.gloss: Hourly/frontline roles CPH benchmark: $1,000-$2,500 per hire
cards.verbatim: By role type, hourly and frontline roles benchmark at $1,000 to $2,500 per hire
