cards.gloss: Manager/director positions run higher CPH still
cards.verbatim: manager/director positions run higher still[16].

cards.gloss: Indeed job-sponsorship minimum is around $150
cards.verbatim: Job advertising costs vary by platform and region: sponsoring a job on Indeed has a minimum of around $150

cards.gloss: LinkedIn ads run roughly $5-9 per click
cards.verbatim: LinkedIn ads run roughly $5-9 per click[19].

cards.gloss: Monthly job-ad spend for a single role in competitive markets can run $500-$2,000+
cards.verbatim: In competitive markets, monthly job-ad spend for a single role can run $500 to $2,000 or more

cards.gloss: Multinational firms invest in localized job boards/region-specific campaigns, adding cost
cards.verbatim: multinational firms hiring globally often invest in localized job boards or region-specific social media campaigns, adding further to cost[19].

cards.gloss: Recruitment agency fees for executive/niche hiring run 15-25% of salary
cards.verbatim: Recruitment agency fees for executive or niche hiring run 15-25% of the position's salary[35].

cards.gloss: Entry-level roles rely on lower-cost broad job board postings and university career sites
cards.verbatim: entry-level roles rely on lower-cost broad job board postings and university career sites

cards.gloss: Mid-level roles need costlier targeted ads or professional network promotion
cards.verbatim: mid-level roles need more targeted (and costlier) ads or professional network promotion

cards.gloss: Executive searches handled by specialized recruiters whose fee covers sourcing, lowering direct ad cost despite high overall fee
cards.verbatim: executive searches are typically handled by specialized recruiters whose fee often covers much of the sourcing work, making direct advertising cost comparatively lower even though the overall search fee is high[19].

cards.gloss: International CPH calculation is more complex depending on contractor/EOR/owned-entity structure
cards.verbatim: For companies hiring internationally, cost-per-hire calculation becomes more complex because the costs sitting inside recruiting CPH versus ongoing employment cost change depending on whether the company uses contractors, an Employer of Record (EOR), or owned legal entities[16].

cards.gloss: EOR hiring shifts some domestic-internal costs to external, adjacent-but-not-part-of recruiting cost
cards.verbatim: When hiring through an EOR, some costs that would be internal in a domestic hire become external, since the EOR handles local compliance, payroll setup, and employment contracts — costs that are adjacent to, but not part of, the recruiting cost figure[16].

cards.gloss: Companies undercount true international hiring cost by missing structural setup costs before first payroll
cards.verbatim: Analysis of mid-market global employment patterns shows companies often undercount the true cost of international hiring because they fail to capture structural setup costs that precede the first payroll

cards.gloss: Overall trend: cost-per-hire benchmarks have risen across re-benchmarking cycles
cards.verbatim: Cost-per-hire benchmarks have moved upward in successive re-benchmarking cycles rather than holding steady.

cards.gloss: SHRM's $4,700 average cost-per-hire figure and its own flag that it is outdated
cards.verbatim: SHRM's widely cited average cost per hire stood at $4,700 for several years, a figure SHRM itself has flagged as reflecting “a prior SHRM benchmarking cycle” that has since been superseded[18].

cards.gloss: One source dates $4,700 baseline to 2024, frames as 14% increase over pre-pandemic
cards.verbatim: One source dates that $4,700 baseline to 2024 and frames it as a 14% increase over pre-pandemic levels[29],

cards.gloss: Another source treats $4,700 as outdated, replaced by $5,475 for non-executive roles
cards.verbatim: another treats it as the outdated reference point that SHRM's 2025 Benchmarking Report update replaced with $5,475 for non-executive roles[18].

cards.gloss: SHRM's 2025 release explicitly updates its prior 2022 benchmarking studies
cards.verbatim: explicitly updating SHRM's prior 2022 benchmarking studies[34].

cards.gloss: 2025 SHRM executive hire cost: $35,879 average, up 21% from 2022
cards.verbatim: Under the 2025 SHRM figures, executive hires cost $35,879 on average, a number reported as up 21% from 2022[18],

cards.gloss: Executive hires described as nearly 7x more expensive than nonexecutive hires (SHRM)
cards.verbatim: separately described as nearly 7x more expensive than nonexecutive hires in SHRM's updated research[34].

cards.gloss: 2024-dated figure: average executive cost per hire of $28,329
cards.verbatim: A different, 2024-dated figure puts average executive-level cost per hire at $28,329[29],

cards.gloss: Another source cites executive costs reaching upwards of $28,000 per hire
cards.verbatim: yet another source cites executive costs “reaching upwards of $28,000 per hire”[12]

cards.gloss: Executive cost figures cluster in the same rough band but are reported inconsistently across sources
cards.verbatim: all pointing to the same rough band but illustrating how the number has been reported differently across cycles and sources.

cards.gloss: Older estimate: executive cost-per-hire multiplier roughly 6x non-executive baseline (2024 figures)
cards.verbatim: Older estimates placed the executive cost-per-hire multiplier at roughly 6x the non-executive baseline given the $4,700-to-$28,329 comparison implied in the 2024 figures[29],

cards.gloss: 2025 figures imply roughly 6.5x executive-to-non-executive cost multiplier
cards.verbatim: versus roughly 6.5x under the 2025 $5,475-to-$35,879 comparison[18].

cards.gloss: Appcast found cost-per-application and cost-per-hire rose sharply in 2025 despite a softer labor market
cards.verbatim: Appcast's Recruitment Marketing Benchmark Report found that both cost-per-application and cost-per-hire rose sharply in 2025 “despite a softer labor market,”

cards.gloss: Appcast attributes the rise to job board pricing and programmatic ad model shifts, not hiring demand
cards.verbatim: attributing the increase to shifts in job board pricing and programmatic ad models rather than to hiring demand[18].

cards.gloss: SHRM attributes its $4,700-to-$5,475 rise to recruiter pay, sourcing complexity, and job board pricing
cards.verbatim: The 2025 SHRM update itself attributes the rise from $4,700 to $5,475 to rising recruiter compensation, greater sourcing complexity, and shifting job board pricing models[18].

cards.gloss: Median U.S. cost per hire reported separately at approximately $1,633
cards.verbatim: Median cost per hire in the U.S., by contrast, has been reported separately at approximately $1,633[12]

cards.gloss: Median is far below SHRM's mean because high-cost hires skew the average upward
cards.verbatim: a figure far below the SHRM mean, reflecting that a small number of high-cost (often executive or specialized) hires pull the average upward relative to the median.

cards.gloss: Ericsson case: cut cost per hire by 70% via social media and employee advocacy, also improved retention
cards.verbatim: On the cost-reduction side, at least one case example shows movement in the opposite direction — Ericsson reportedly cut its cost per hire by 70% through social media and employee advocacy initiatives, which also improved retention[12]

cards.gloss: AI recruiting tools now used to cut average cost per hire by 30% or more
cards.verbatim: and current guidance points to AI recruiting tools as a lever now being used to cut average cost per hire by 30% or more, in contrast to the historically manual, and increasingly expensive, recruiting processes described above[18].

cards.gloss: Recruitment cost varies sharply by channel/method used
cards.verbatim: Recruitment spend varies sharply by the channel or method used to fill a role, with agency-based hiring, job board advertising, and employee referrals producing very different cost profiles per hire.

cards.gloss: Job board/ad fees are a baseline external cost across most methods
cards.verbatim: Job board and advertising fees form a baseline external cost across nearly every recruitment method, covering postings on platforms, social media promotions, and sponsored content[12][20][8].

cards.gloss: Job posting cost is small for entry-level, climbs for hard-to-fill roles
cards.verbatim: This upfront cost is relatively small for entry-level roles — often just a few hundred dollars in job postings — but can climb substantially for hard-to-fill positions[19].

cards.gloss: Job boards need a high volume of applicants per hire (50-60)
cards.verbatim: Job boards typically require a high volume of applicants relative to hires: companies often need over 50-60 applicants per hire when sourcing through job boards[36].

cards.gloss: Job board fees often billed annually; must divide by period for per-hire cost
cards.verbatim: Fees are frequently structured annually rather than per post, which requires dividing the usage cost by the applicable calculation period to get an accurate per-hire figure[37].

cards.gloss: Recommendation to track cost per hire by channel, not just upfront cost
cards.verbatim: Not every channel produces hires at the same cost, and tracking cost per hire by channel — job boards, referrals, agencies, talent communities, career site traffic, and outbound sourcing — is recommended so that a channel that looks expensive upfront can still be judged efficient if it produces faster, higher-quality hires, while a cheap channel can prove costly if it fills the funnel with low-fit applicants that waste recruiter and manager time[9].

cards.gloss: Agency/headhunter fees are typically 15-25% of salary
cards.verbatim: Agency and headhunter fees represent one of the largest direct costs in recruitment, typically running 15-25% of the hire's salary as a contingency search fee[8][1].

cards.gloss: Entry-level roles: companies often avoid agencies to save money
cards.verbatim: Many companies avoid agencies for junior roles to save money

cards.gloss: Entry-level agency fee example: 20% of $30,000 = $6,000
cards.verbatim: when agencies are used (e.g., for volume or specialized hiring), a fee of roughly 20% of a $30,000 salary works out to about $6,000[19].

cards.gloss: Mid-level roles often filled via agencies at 15-25% fee
cards.verbatim: Very often filled via agencies or headhunters, where the 15-25% fee comes into play[19].

cards.gloss: Executive roles almost always use external recruiters, at high cost
cards.verbatim: External recruiters are almost always used for high-level executive roles, at a high cost

cards.gloss: Executive agency fee example: 30% of $200,000 = $60,000
cards.verbatim: for an executive earning $200,000, a 30% fee equals $60,000, which can dwarf every other hiring cost combined[19].

cards.gloss: Agency fees worthwhile for speed/specialization but raise cost-per-hire
cards.verbatim: Agency fees are described as worthwhile when fast results or industry-specific talent are needed, but they drastically increase cost-per-hire, and companies must weigh this against internal recruitment capacity[19].

cards.gloss: External cost categories beyond agency fees
cards.verbatim: Beyond agency fees, external costs broadly include job board fees, recruitment agency fees, background checks and drug screenings, employer branding spend, career fairs and recruiting events, and candidate travel or reimbursed expenses[9].

cards.gloss: Nature's Pride case: bringing recruitment in-house cut ~$1,100/hire
cards.verbatim: A real-world example: Nature's Pride found that as its business grew, relying on external recruitment agencies did not build the strength of its internal recruitment team; choosing to bring recruitment fully in-house instead resulted in an approximate drop of $1,100 per hire[11].

cards.gloss: Internal recruiting costs driven by in-house labor, not external fees
cards.verbatim: Internal recruiting costs are driven primarily by the labor of the in-house team rather than external fees.

cards.gloss: Internal TA specialist salary cost works out to ~$2,000 per hire
cards.verbatim: An internal Talent Acquisition specialist earning $60,000-$80,000 per year who handles roughly 40 hires annually works out to about $2,000 per hire in salary cost alone, before counting the added time of hiring managers and interview panel members[19].

cards.gloss: Broader internal cost categories list
cards.verbatim: Broader internal cost categories include recruiter salaries and benefits, hiring manager time spent reviewing candidates and interviewing, recruiting technology (ATS, video interview platforms, assessment tools), employee referral bonuses, and internal training for recruiters or interviewers[9].

cards.gloss: SHRM/ANSI standard's definition of internal costs
cards.verbatim: The SHRM/ANSI standard frames internal costs as the staff, capital, and organizational costs of the recruiting function, including fully loaded recruiting salaries and talent acquisition system costs[9].

cards.gloss: Employee referrals are the most cost-effective recruitment method
cards.verbatim: Employee referrals stand out as the most cost-effective recruitment method across the sources.

cards.gloss: Referral programs yield higher-quality candidates, shorten hiring
cards.verbatim: Referral programs are highly cost-effective, often yielding higher-quality candidates who stay longer and shortening the hiring process[12].

cards.gloss: ERIN study: roughly 1 in 10 referrals results in a hire
cards.verbatim: According to an ERIN study, among enterprise-level organizations, roughly 1 in 10 referrals results in a hire — a conversion rate significantly higher than job boards, where companies often need over 50-60 applicants per hire[36].

cards.gloss: ERIN study referral funnel breakdown (10 → 1 hire)
cards.verbatim: The same study detailed a referral funnel: out of 10 candidates who receive a referral notice, eight respond, six apply, four are interviewed, and one is hired[36].

cards.gloss: JLL case: referral platform volume (employees and referrals made)
cards.verbatim: At JLL, after going live with a referral platform for a little over four months, more than 13,500 employees made over 11,000 referrals

cards.gloss: JLL case: applications generated and offers resulting
cards.verbatim: generating over 13,000 referral applications (some applying to multiple roles) and resulting in over 600 offers[36].

cards.gloss: SHRM org case: about 50% of referrals become hires
cards.verbatim: At a smaller organization like SHRM, with roughly 500 employees, about 50% of referrals become hires

cards.gloss: SHRM org case: 10%+ of 2024 hires came from referrals
cards.verbatim: in 2024, slightly more than 10% of all hires came from employee referrals[36].

cards.gloss: Referred candidates need fewer interviews; referral bonus costs less
cards.verbatim: Because referred candidates come pre-vetted by trusted employees, they may require fewer interview rounds or assessments, and even a modest referral bonus tends to cost less overall than traditional sourcing methods[10].

cards.gloss: Internal mobility saves external recruitment costs, faster integration
cards.verbatim: Hiring from within saves significant costs associated with external recruitment, including advertising and agency fees, and often leads to faster integration than external hires[12].

cards.gloss: Succession planning improves retention rates
cards.verbatim: Proactive succession planning that prepares internal candidates for future openings is credited with improving retention rates significantly[12].

cards.gloss: Standard cost-per-hire formula
cards.verbatim: Regardless of method mix, the standard formula for cost per hire is total recruiting costs (internal plus external) divided by number of hires[12][8][9].

cards.gloss: SHRM 2025 benchmark: average cost per hire ~$4,700
cards.verbatim: SHRM's 2025 industry benchmark puts the average cost per hire in the United States at around $4,700[12][19]

cards.gloss: Worked example: $50k internal + $30k external over 20 hires = $4,000/hire
cards.verbatim: one worked example using a $50,000 internal cost plus $30,000 external cost over 20 hires yields $4,000 per hire[12]

cards.gloss: Worked example: $100,000 to hire 50 people = $2,000/hire
cards.verbatim: another example of $100,000 spent to hire 50 people yields $2,000 per hire[11].

cards.gloss: SHRM: hidden costs can push total hiring cost to 3-4x salary
cards.verbatim: SHRM further notes that when hidden costs like lost productivity are included, total hiring cost can reach 3-4 times the position's salary

cards.gloss: Example: a $60,000 job can effectively cost $180,000 with hidden costs
cards.verbatim: meaning a $60,000 job might effectively cost $180,000 by the time the new hire is fully productive[19].

cards.gloss: Referrals are a highly cost-effective, pre-vetted hiring channel
cards.verbatim: Referrals are consistently identified as one of the most cost-effective hiring channels, with pre-vetted candidates that require fewer interview or assessment rounds[10][12].

cards.gloss: Jobvite: referrals cut cost per hire up to 50%
cards.verbatim: Jobvite research found employee referrals can decrease cost per hire by up to 50%[38].

cards.gloss: LinkedIn: referred employees retain 45% better
cards.verbatim: LinkedIn research found referred employees have a 45% higher retention rate than employees hired through other channels[38].

cards.gloss: Referral savings estimate ~$3,000/hire, 70% longer tenure
cards.verbatim: A separate estimate places referral savings at approximately $3,000 per new hire, with referred employees staying 70% longer[8].

cards.gloss: ERIN 2024 data: referral volume and 1-in-10 hire conversion rate
cards.verbatim: ERIN, an employee referral platform, analyzed 2024 data covering over 1.1 million referrals from 744,580 unique users across enterprise organizations, finding that 1 in 10 referrals results in a hire — a materially higher conversion rate than job boards, which often require 50–60 applicants per hire[36].

cards.gloss: ERIN referral funnel breakdown
cards.verbatim: The referral funnel breaks down as: out of 10 candidates who receive a referral notice, 8 respond, 6 apply, 4 are interviewed, and 1 is hired[36].

cards.gloss: JLL case study: referral volume after launching ERIN
cards.verbatim: At JLL, just over four months after launching ERIN, more than 13,500 employees made over 11,000 referrals, generating over 13,000 referral applications and resulting in more than 600 offers[36].

cards.gloss: SHRM case study: referral-to-hire conversion and share of hires
cards.verbatim: At SHRM (roughly 500 employees), about 50% of referrals become hires, and in 2024 slightly more than 10% of all hires came through employee referrals[36].

cards.gloss: Referral channel choice affects conversion (email vs social vs SMS)
cards.verbatim: Referral channel matters: 55% of referrals were sent by email, 30% shared via social media, and 10% by SMS/text, but while 30% of all referrals came via social media, only 14% of hires originated from that channel — direct, one-to-one referrals convert better than social shares[36].

cards.gloss: Referral submissions skew desktop and work-hours
cards.verbatim: 55% of ERIN users preferred submitting referrals via desktop rather than mobile, often during work hours, suggesting referral activity is treated as part of the job rather than an afterthought[36].

cards.gloss: SHRM's referral bonus structure and eligibility exclusions
cards.verbatim: SHRM structures its referral bonus as half paid at hire and half at the six-month retention mark, and excludes anyone with influence over the hiring process (including HR) from eligibility[36].

cards.gloss: Common cost-cutting advice (agency fees, job board rates) yields small savings
cards.verbatim: Most guidance on reducing recruitment costs focuses on trimming agency fees and negotiating job board rates, but these savings are real yet comparatively small[25].

cards.gloss: Biggest recruitment cost is invisible re-hiring after a bad hire
cards.verbatim: The largest recruitment cost at most organizations does not show up as a line-item invoice at all: it is the cost of re-hiring after a first hire fails to work out[25].

cards.gloss: Direct vs indirect costs; invoice tracking misses the larger indirect half
cards.verbatim: Direct costs are invoiced and plannable; indirect costs are hidden in lost productivity, vacant roles, and poor hiring decisions, and if an organization only tracks invoices, it is managing the smaller half of its total spend[15].

cards.gloss: SHRM's ~$4,700 cost-per-hire understates true total cost
cards.verbatim: SHRM's widely cited average cost per hire of roughly $4,700 mostly captures direct costs; once recruiter time, lost output, and onboarding are added, the real total often runs two to three times higher[15].

cards.gloss: Gallup/Wharton: replacing an employee costs 50-200% of salary
cards.verbatim: Gallup places the cost of replacing an employee at 50% to 200% of their salary[15], a figure corroborated by a Knowledge at Wharton study using the same 50%–200% range[38].

cards.gloss: Forbes: high first-year and first-90-day quit rates and reasons
cards.verbatim: Forbes' Key HR Statistics And Trends In 2024 found that almost 40% of employees quit within their first year, and over 40% of those leave within the first 90 days, most often citing a lack of career development, disliked job characteristics, or poor work-life balance[38].

cards.gloss: Core strategy reframe: better hiring decisions and retention over cheaper candidates
cards.verbatim: This reframes the core strategy: the most effective way to reduce total recruitment cost is not to find cheaper candidates but to make better hiring decisions and keep the people already hired[25][15].

cards.gloss: A seat re-emptying within 90 days doubles cost; onboarding is a cost lever
cards.verbatim: Because a seat that empties again within 90 days means costs were paid twice, not saved[25], structured onboarding is framed as a direct cost-reduction lever rather than a soft HR nicety.

cards.gloss: FirstHR AI onboarding wizard: structured 90-day plan mechanics
cards.verbatim: One example (FirstHR) uses an AI onboarding wizard that generates a structured 90-day plan for every hire: compliance paperwork (I-9, W-4, handbook) goes out for e-signature before Day 1, training modules deliver role-specific knowledge, and task workflows assign check-ins at Day 7, 30, 60, and 90[25].

cards.gloss: FirstHR outcome: faster productivity, fewer early departures, $98/month cost
cards.verbatim: The stated outcome is new hires productive by Day 30 instead of still "figuring things out" by Day 60, with fewer departures in the first 90 days, delivered at $98/month flat[25].

cards.gloss: Tracking re-hiring rates flags process/role-design problems early
cards.verbatim: More broadly, tracking metrics such as re-hiring rates for specific roles can flag process or role-design problems before they compound into repeated hiring costs[12].

cards.gloss: Strong employer brand lowers cost per hire via organic attraction
cards.verbatim: A strong employer brand reduces cost per hire by attracting qualified candidates organically, lowering reliance on paid advertising[10][8][12].

cards.gloss: Ericsson case: 70% cost-per-hire reduction via social/advocacy
cards.verbatim: Ericsson reduced its cost per hire by 70% through social media and employee advocacy initiatives, with associated high retention rates[8][11].

cards.gloss: LinkedIn: strong employer brands cut cost per hire up to 43%
cards.verbatim: One LinkedIn study found companies with strong employer brands have up to 43% lower cost per hire[12].

cards.gloss: Nokia case: 74% cost-per-hire reduction via Indeed/ATS routing
cards.verbatim: Nokia reduced its cost per hire by 74% compared to its company average by adopting Indeed as its preferred job search engine, with applications routed directly into its applicant tracking system[11][12].

cards.gloss: Nature's Pride case: ~$1,100/hire drop from in-house recruiting
cards.verbatim: Nature's Pride achieved an approximate drop of $1,100 per hire by bringing recruitment fully in-house rather than relying on external agencies, a move driven by exponential growth in hiring needs[8][11].

cards.gloss: AI screening/scheduling cuts cost-per-hire 20-40%
cards.verbatim: AI screening and scheduling can deliver 20–40% lower cost-per-hire[39].

cards.gloss: Average 33% savings in time-to-hire and cost-per-hire
cards.verbatim: Average savings of 33% in both time-to-hire and cost-per-hire have been reported[39].

cards.gloss: Enterprise companies save $2.3M/year via recruitment automation
cards.verbatim: Enterprise companies report saving $2.3 million annually through recruitment automation[39].

cards.gloss: PwC: AI recruitment tools deliver 340% ROI within 18 months
cards.verbatim: PwC found AI recruitment tools can deliver an average 340% ROI within 18 months[39].

cards.gloss: SHRM: AI tools give 31% faster hiring, 50% better quality-of-hire
cards.verbatim: SHRM reports organizations using AI-powered recruitment tools see 31% faster hiring times and a 50% improvement in quality-of-hire metrics[39].

cards.gloss: Automation cuts time-to-hire 30-50%; reclaims ~23 hrs/hire of screening time
cards.verbatim: Automation reduces time-to-hire by 30–50% per Deloitte and other studies[39]; recruiters traditionally spend up to 23 hours per hire on manual screening, time automation can reclaim[39].

cards.gloss: 85% of employers using AI/automation report increased efficiency
cards.verbatim: 85% of employers using AI/automation report increased efficiency (SHRM)[39].

cards.gloss: Adoption stats: 73% investing in automation; AI-in-HR adoption 43% in 2025
cards.verbatim: Adoption context: over 73% of companies are investing in recruitment automation tools; AI adoption in HR climbed to 43% in 2025, up from 26% in 2024 (SHRM)[39].

cards.gloss: AI recruitment market projected to $1.12B by 2030; 81% plan to invest by 2027
cards.verbatim: The AI recruitment market is projected to reach $1.12 billion by 2030, and 81% of companies plan to invest in AI-driven recruiting solutions by 2027 (Gartner)[39].

cards.gloss: 51% of orgs already use AI for resume screening and job description writing
cards.verbatim: 51% of organizations already use AI for tasks like resume screening (44% of that group) and job description writing (66%) (SHRM)[39].

cards.gloss: Basic ROI formula for automation investment
cards.verbatim: A basic ROI framework for evaluating automation investment: ROI = (Value Generated − Total Costs) / Total Costs × 100[39].

cards.gloss: Costs to include in automation ROI calc
cards.verbatim: Costs to include: software subscriptions and implementation, training and change management, and integration with existing ATS/HCM systems[39].

cards.gloss: How to quantify value in automation ROI calc
cards.verbatim: Value should be quantified via time-to-hire reduction (hours saved × recruiter hourly rate), cost-per-hire savings tracked pre- and post-automation, quality-of-hire measured through performance ratings and retention (first-year retention up 20–30% in some cases), and productivity gains from freed recruiter hours[39].

cards.gloss: Worked ROI example numbers
cards.verbatim: Worked example: an annual automation tool cost of $50,000 against a 40% reduction in time-to-hire ($200,000 saved) plus improved hire quality ($150,000 in retained value) yields an ROI calculation based on $350,000 in generated value[39].

cards.gloss: ATS reduces administrative overhead across the hiring pipeline
cards.verbatim: Applicant Tracking Systems (ATS) streamline job posting, resume screening, interview scheduling, and candidate data management, reducing administrative overhead[20][10][5][12].

cards.gloss: Skills-based hiring platforms verify competencies, some pay-per-hire
cards.verbatim: Skills-based hiring platforms verify competencies via assessments, often providing pre-screened candidate pools that reduce screening time and cost; some operate on pay-per-hire models[12].

cards.gloss: Pre-employment assessments reduce bad-hire risk
cards.verbatim: Pre-employment assessments help gauge skill and role fit, reducing the risk of a bad hire[5].

cards.gloss: Market intelligence keeps offers competitive, reduces turnover
cards.verbatim: Market intelligence — tracking salary trends, skill demand, and compensation benchmarks — helps keep offers competitive, reducing costly turnover[5].

cards.gloss: Benchmark cost per hire by industry/role, not one company-wide target
cards.verbatim: Organizations should benchmark cost per hire against industry- and role-specific standards rather than a single company-wide target, since specialized roles (e.g., actuarial scientists, senior technical positions) can reasonably carry higher costs[8].

cards.gloss: Remote roles trade travel/relocation savings for other new costs
cards.verbatim: Recruitment costs for remote roles differ from in-office roles: relocation and travel costs for interviews may be reduced or eliminated, but this can be offset by additional costs for technology setup, virtual onboarding, and managing a distributed team[5].

cards.gloss: Low CPH with high turnover/long time-to-fill signals under-investment
cards.verbatim: a low cost per hire paired with high turnover or long time-to-fill may signal under-investment rather than efficiency

cards.gloss: Low CPH isn't always good — can mean under-investing in employer brand
cards.verbatim: low CPH "isn't always good" because it can indicate under-investing in employer brand, leading to weak pipelines and eventual quality problems[16]

cards.gloss: Recommended fix: pair CPH with a quality signal
cards.verbatim: The recommended fix is pairing CPH with a quality signal — a 90-day retention rate or hiring-manager satisfaction score

cards.gloss: Cutting CPH without tracking quality raises downstream costs
cards.verbatim: reducing cost per hire without tracking quality can increase downstream replacement hiring and total labor cost[16]

cards.gloss: Goal reframed: right number, not lowest number
cards.verbatim: This reframes the goal explicitly: "you're not optimising for the lowest number. You're optimising for the right number given your quality requirements"[16].

cards.gloss: Easy-to-fill roles skew blended CPH average downward, hiding costs
cards.verbatim: A related caution is that a high volume of easy-to-fill roles can skew a blended average downward, meaning organizations "have hidden costs rather than eliminated costs"[16].

cards.gloss: A single blended CPH figure hides the real story across functions
cards.verbatim: A single blended cost-per-hire figure "can hide the real story," since engineering, sales, customer support, and operations roles behave differently

cards.gloss: Recommendation to segment CPH by function
cards.verbatim: segmenting by function is recommended to find where costs are actually concentrated[9]

cards.gloss: Open disagreement about the real average CPH figure
cards.verbatim: There is open disagreement about what the "real" average cost per hire even is.

cards.gloss: SHRM's commonly cited $4,700 benchmark described as out of date
cards.verbatim: The commonly cited SHRM benchmark of $4,700 across all industries[10] is described elsewhere as out of date

cards.gloss: Current SHRM benchmark reportedly noticeably higher
cards.verbatim: current SHRM benchmarks reportedly putting "the real figure noticeably higher"[9]

cards.gloss: Founder's comment: companies only know invoice-visible hiring costs
cards.verbatim: "Most companies don't actually know what hiring costs them. They only know what they can see on the invoice"[9]

cards.gloss: Even updated SHRM figure only captures invoice-visible cost
cards.verbatim: the updated, higher SHRM figure is characterized as only capturing what shows up on an invoice, not the fuller cost[9]

cards.gloss: SHRM benchmark for cost to replace an employee: 0.5x-2x salary
cards.verbatim: SHRM's own benchmark for average cost to replace an employee is cited as ranging from one-half to two times the employee's annual salary[27]

cards.gloss: Example: $60,000 manager implies up to $120,000 replacement cost
cards.verbatim: which for a $60,000 manager implies total replacement costs up to $120,000[27]

cards.gloss: Replacement-cost benchmark hard to reconcile with flat CPH figure
cards.verbatim: a figure that is hard to reconcile with a flat $4,700-$4,800 "cost per hire" statistic, pointing to inconsistency in what different benchmarks actually measure (replacement cost vs. hiring cost vs. cost per hire narrowly defined).

cards.gloss: Role-level benchmark: typical hires $6k-$15k, VP+ $15k-$50k+
cards.verbatim: one figure places typical hires at $6,000–$15,000, with executive roles at VP level and above commonly reaching $15,000–$50,000+[16]

cards.gloss: Separate $240,000 figure for upper-range executive bad hires (CareerBuilder)
cards.verbatim: another source separately cites a $240,000 figure representing the upper range for executive-level bad hires when factoring in all associated costs, drawn from CareerBuilder's "The State of Recruiting" reports from 2014–2024[29]

cards.gloss: Central debate over what counts as cost per hire
cards.verbatim: A central debate is over scope: what should be included in "cost per hire" at all.

cards.gloss: Direct vs indirect cost breakdown defined

cards.gloss: An 8-point playbook for lowering cost per hire: referrals, in-house sourcing, candidate experience, AI tools, faster time-to-fill, source ROI tracking, agency audits, and talent pools.
cards.verbatim:
1. Invest in employee referrals. Referrals consistently produce lower CPH and higher quality of hire than agency hires. Typical referral CPH is 30-60% of overall average.
- Build internal sourcing capability. In-house sourcers using LinkedIn Recruiter, SeekOut, and similar tools reduce agency dependence. Mature TA teams run 70%+ direct-sourced.
- Optimise candidate experience. Lower drop-off improves yield ratios; the same volume of applications produces more hires.
- Use AI tools for high-leverage activities. Resume screening, candidate matching, interview scheduling. Per industry research, AI recruiting tools cut average CPH by 30%+ in mature implementations.
- Reduce time-to-fill. Vacancy cost is often larger than CPH; reducing time-to-fill compounds savings.
- Track source-of-hire ROI rigorously. Quality-adjusted CPH per source is the right metric.
- Audit agency relationships. Are contingent fees justified by hire outcomes? Many agency hires could be made direct.
- Build talent pools. Pre-existing talent pipelines reduce future CPH dramatically.

cards.gloss: Lists common cost-per-hire measurement mistakes, such as undercounting costs, ignoring vacancy cost, and optimizing for cost over quality, with links to related glossary terms.
cards.verbatim:
- Undercounting by 30-50%. Per SHRM 2025 benchmarking, organisations using the full ANSI/SHRM methodology reported costs 34% higher than their previously self-reported figures.
- Ignoring vacancy cost. CPH benchmarks compare like-to-like, but the real cost often includes vacancy productivity loss exceeding the recruiting investment.
- Optimising CPH at the expense of quality. Cheapest hires often don’t perform; quality-adjusted CPH is the right metric.
- Including only successful searches. Under SHRM/ANSI, all recruiting costs in a period should be divided by all hires in that period.
- Treating CPH as a stand-alone KPI. Measure alongside time-to-fill, quality-of-hire, candidate experience, and source-of-hire effectiveness.
- Comparing across companies without controls. Industry, role mix, geography, and methodology all affect CPH; apples-to-apples comparisons require careful normalisation.

cards.gloss: FAQ answering what cost per hire is, how to calculate it, and what the average 2026 CPH figures are by role level.
cards.verbatim:
What is cost per hire?
Cost per hire (CPH) is the standardised talent acquisition metric measuring the total investment required to source, attract, assess, and onboard a new employee. The authoritative SHRM/ANSI formula is: CPH = (Total Internal Recruiting Costs + Total External Recruiting Costs) / Total Number of Hires. Per SHRM 2026 Talent Access Benchmarking Report, average US CPH is approximately $4,700-$4,800 for non-executive roles and $28,329-$35,879 for executive hires.
How do you calculate cost per hire?
Use the SHRM/ANSI formula: CPH = (Internal Costs + External Costs) / Total Hires. Internal costs include recruiter salaries and overhead, hiring manager and interviewer time, HR administrative time, recruiting technology (ATS, sourcing tools), internal referral bonuses, and recruiting events. External costs include job board postings, recruitment advertising, agency or retained search fees, background checks and assessments, sign-on bonuses, relocation, and candidate travel. Divide all recruiting costs in a period by all hires made in that same period.
What’s the average cost per hire in 2026?
Per SHRM 2026 Talent Access Benchmarking Report: approximately $4,700-$4,800 for non-executive roles (US average). Executive roles average $28,329-$35,879 (up 21% from 2022). Significant variation by role: entry-level $1,500-$3,500; mid-level professional $3,500-$8,000; engineering $6,000-$23,000; senior management $10,000-$30,000; retained executive search $50,000-$250,000. Technology and financial services above average; retail and hospitality below average.
What costs are missing from the SHRM cost per hire formula?
The SHRM/ANSI formula does not include vacancy cost (productivity loss while a role sits empty), which is often larger than the recruiting investment. Per industry research: standard professional roles lose ~$500/day; revenue-generating sales roles lose $7,000-$10,000/month. With median 2026 US time-to-fill at 63.5 days, vacancy cost typically adds $22,000+ to the SHRM CPH for standard roles. Also excluded: ramp cost (new hires below full productivity for 3-12 months) and quality risk.
How do you reduce cost per hire?
Invest in employee referrals (consistently lowest CPH and highest quality), build internal sourcing capability (reduce agency dependence), optimise candidate experience (lower drop-off improves yield), use AI tools (mature implementations cut CPH 30%+), reduce time-to-fill (compounds savings via vacancy cost), track source-of-hire ROI rigorously, audit agency relationships, and build talent pools (pre-engaged candidates reduce future CPH dramatically).
Is a lower cost per hire always better?
No. If low-CPH hires leave quickly or underperform, the true hiring cost is much higher. CPH should be tracked alongside quality-of-hire, time-to-fill, candidate experience, source-of-hire effectiveness, and 90-day / 1-year retention. Quality-adjusted CPH, the cost per successful, retained, and productive hire, is the metric that matters for business outcomes.

A single mis-hire can trigger a cascade of voluntary exits among high performers. The pattern: the mis-hire underperforms, high performers absorb extra workload, morale drops, and within 3-6 months 1-2 of those high performers leave for roles with less friction.

Organizations tracking assessment impact KPIs consistently find that every 1 involuntary exit at manager level correlates with 0.8-1.2 voluntary exits in the same team within the next quarter.

Evaluating candidates for values and culture alignment – not just hard skills – reduces this multiplier. It is one of the foundational pillars of a talent management strategy that compounds over time.

The Testlify Mis-Hire Cost Stack is a 5-layer model for calculating the total cost of a hiring mistake. Most organizations calculate only Layer 1. The full stack typically runs 2.5-4x that estimate.

 Layer 1 – Recruitment Spend 
Job ads + agency fees + interviewer hours + ATS costs. Average: $4,700-$15,000 per role.

 Layer 2 – Onboarding and Training Investment 
Equipment + HR onboarding time + L&D programs + manager ramp support. Average: $1,500-$5,000.

 Layer 3 – Lost Productivity 
Role vacancy equivalent + ramp shortfall + error correction time. Equals 3-6 months of salary cost.

 Layer 4 – Team and Culture Damage 
Morale impact x team size x 8-12% output reduction across a 5-person team for 60-90 days.

 Layer 5 – Revenue and Client Impact 
Missed pipeline, delayed projects, client relationship gaps. Most severe in sales, client-facing, and product roles.

 Formula: 
Total Mis-Hire Cost = Layer 1 + Layer 2 + Layer 3 + Layer 4 + Layer 5

For a manager-level role at $120,000/year, a full-stack calculation typically lands between $300,000-$600,000 – not the $4,700 cost-per-hire figure most ATS dashboards report.

cards.gloss: Explains that recruitment budgets spiral not from one expensive channel but from repeatedly investing time/money in candidates who were never a fit.
cards.verbatim:
Recruitment costs rarely spiral because of a single expensive channel. Budgets grow when money and time are repeatedly invested in candidates who never had a realistic chance of being hired.

Every unnecessary application, interview, and replacement hire adds another layer of avoidable cost. To control recruiting spend, start by identifying where the budget leaks occur most often.
cards.heading: Why does recruitment cost spiral beyond budget?

cards.gloss: Job board and agency fees reward volume over fit, costing $9k-$15k per placement; skills screening before interviews is where the ROI is.
cards.verbatim:
Both paid job boards and agency placements reward volume over fit, which is why cost per hire keeps climbing even when the labor market cools. A 15-25% agency fee on a $60,000 role costs $9,000 to $15,000 per placement regardless of whether the hire lasts 90 days.

Adding a skills screening step before any interview invite converts a 50-person unscreened pool into an 8-12-person shortlisted pool before any calendar time is consumed. That is where the ROI on assessment spend sits.
cards.heading: Job board and agency fees

cards.gloss: Quantifies hiring manager interview time as a hidden cost (~$4,500 per role) that doesn't show up on sourcing invoices.
cards.verbatim:
A recruiter managing 15 open roles who schedules three interviews per role per round burns over 45 hours of senior calendar time before a single offer goes out. At a blended loaded rate of $100 per hour, that is $4,500 in interview labor per role before any sourcing fees are counted.

This cost does not appear on a sourcing invoice, which is why most finance teams miss it. Tracking interview hours per role alongside cost per hire reveals where the real budget drain is.
cards.heading: Hiring manager time as a hidden cost driver

cards.gloss: Notes that the highest-volume sourcing channel often produces the most expensive mis-hires, so budget should shift toward filtering, not just spending less.
cards.verbatim:
A pattern we keep observing in enterprise TA teams: the most expensive mis-hires come through the same job board that received the largest slice of the sourcing budget. High applicant volume looks like success until the 90-day attrition data arrives.

The fix is not always to spend less. Redirect budget from the channels producing low-signal volume toward the filters that stop unqualified candidates from consuming interview hours.
cards.heading: The sourcing-to-failure mismatch

cards.gloss: Cites Gallup data on the cost of replacing an employee (0.5x-2x salary) and the $1 trillion aggregate US turnover cost.
cards.verbatim: Gallup research puts the cost of replacing a single employee at between half and twice their annual salary. For a role paying $75,000, that range runs from $37,500 to $150,000 per restart, and U.S. employers collectively absorb $1 trillion in voluntary turnover costs every year.
cards.heading: What does a bad hire actually cost?

cards.gloss: Breaks down direct replacement costs (sourcing, recruiter time, interviewing) as 30-75% of annual salary and suggests benchmarking your own 90-day attrition rate.
cards.verbatim:
Direct replacement costs include sourcing fees, recruiter time, assessment costs, and interviewing overhead. For a senior individual contributor, these visible costs typically land between 30% and 75% of annual salary.

Those figures vary significantly by role seniority and industry. Your own 90-day attrition rate by source is a more useful benchmark than any industry average, because it reflects the actual failure rate of your specific process.

cards.gloss: Shows how bad-hire costs compound over time via a worked example, and argues a wrong-fit hire who stays can cost more than one who leaves early.
cards.verbatim:
A 90-day exit on an $80,000 role requiring two sourcing rounds, six interviews, and three weeks of onboarding carries a real cost closer to $60,000 to $80,000 when time-to-productivity loss and bench productivity impact are included. The cost of a bad hire is best understood as a multiplier, not a fixed number.

A wrong-fit hire who stays is often more expensive than one who exits at 90 days. A disengaged employee has a measurable drag on team output, on top of the eventual replacement cost that arrives later.
cards.heading: How bad hire costs compound over time

cards.gloss: Table plus explanation of the four dominant preventable cost drivers (job board/agency fees, interview hours, bad-hire replacement, onboarding waste) and their reduction levers.
cards.verbatim:
Most organizations have three or four dominant cost drivers; the rest is noise. Job board fees, agency placements, hiring manager interview time, and onboarding waste from wrong-fit hires account for the majority of preventable spend.

 Cost Component What Drives It Practical Reduction Lever 
 Job board/agency fees High applicant volume with low quality signal Add skills screening before sourcing spend; build referral pipeline 
 Interview hours (hiring manager time) Wide unscreened funnel, multiple rounds Screen-first model; one structured interview round replaces three gut-check calls 
 Bad hire replacement Poor competency matching at hire stage Objective test scores before any interview shortlist is built 
 Onboarding waste Wrong-fit hires reach 30+ days before failing Shortlist from assessment results, not resume impressions alone 
 Early attrition (first 90 days) Mismatched expectations or role fit Pre-hire assessments clarify role demands; quality-of-hire metrics catch patterns early 

Agency fees and job board spend are visible and easy to cut. Interview hours and onboarding waste are harder to measure but often larger in aggregate, which is why optimizing only the visible line items misses most of the opportunity.

cards.gloss: Introduces three consistent cost-reduction levers: earlier screening, referrals/internal mobility, and structured interviews, best applied together.
cards.verbatim: Three levers work consistently across enterprise TA teams: screening earlier compresses interview overhead, referrals and internal mobility replace expensive sourcing channels, and structured interviews cut decision time without reducing rigor. Applying only one lever in isolation leaves most of the savings on the table.
cards.heading: How to reduce recruitment costs?

cards.gloss: Details building a referral program with $500-$1,500 bonuses paid within 30 days, saving thousands versus agency fees.
cards.verbatim:
A referral bonus of $500 to $1,500 per successful hire compares to an agency fee of 15-25% of first-year salary. For a $60,000 role, that is a saving of $9,000 to $15,000 per hire versus an agency placement, one of the highest-ROI investments available to any TA budget.

Two things kill referral programs: slow bonus payment and a painful submission process. Pay within 30 days of the new hire’s start date and keep the nomination to a single form.
cards.heading: Build a structured employee referral program

cards.gloss: Advocates checking internal mobility/skill-gap analysis before external sourcing to fill roles at lower cost with existing staff.
cards.verbatim:
Internal mobility is the zero-cost sourcing channel most enterprise teams underuse. A skill gap analysis run across your current workforce before any external search often surfaces two or three internal candidates who could fill the role with 60 to 90 days of targeted development.

You eliminate sourcing cost entirely and retain someone who already understands your systems and culture. The development investment is almost always lower than the replacement cost of an external hire.

 Pro Tip: Before cutting any recruiting line item, map where your spend concentrates against where your failures happen. If 80% of your sourcing spend produces candidates who wash out at the phone screen stage, the problem is not budget size; it is where the first quality filter sits. Fix the filter position before reducing the budget, or you will produce a smaller pool of the same low-signal candidates.

cards.gloss: Introduces Testlify's four-step Screen-First Hiring Model and the applicant-volume conditions where it works best.
cards.verbatim:
The Screen-First Hiring Model is a four-step sequence where hiring managers only meet candidates who have already demonstrated core competency for the role. Each step answers one question before the next begins, which is what makes it faster and cheaper than a traditional funnel where competency questions are deferred to interviews.

The model works best for roles receiving 20 or more applications where competency is the primary differentiator. Very senior executive searches and highly specialized roles with single-digit applicant volumes have different funnel economics.

cards.gloss: Step 3: shortlist only the top 15-20% of assessment scorers, cutting a 50-person pool to 8-10 interview candidates.
cards.verbatim:
Review only the top 15 to 20% of applicants who complete the assessment. For a 50-application pool, that means 8 to 10 candidates go to interview: enough for a confident decision without creating a second full round of overhead.

 Skills assessments improve the recruitment process most visibly at this step, where the shortlist is built on demonstrated ability rather than recruiter intuition or resume formatting. That distinction matters for both quality of hire and legal defensibility.
cards.heading: Step 3: Shortlist from top scorers only

cards.gloss: Step 4: run one structured interview round with a shared scorecard, cutting time-to-fill and offer-stage dropout.
cards.verbatim:
Every interviewer uses the same scorecard and rates the same dimensions, so consensus happens without a separate resolution session. One 60-minute structured interview often replaces three separate rounds, cutting five to ten days off average time to fill.

Offer-stage dropout also falls because candidates who have invested meaningfully in the process and received a consistent interviewing experience are less likely to ghost or withdraw after an offer.
cards.heading: Step 4: One structured interview round

cards.gloss: Explains how referrals and structured interviews each cut costs (bonus vs agency fee, one scorecard round vs three), citing Gallup engagement/profitability stats.
cards.verbatim:
Referrals cut sourcing costs by replacing a 15-25% agency fee with a $500 to $1,500 referral bonus. Structured interviews cut interview overhead by replacing three disconnected rounds with one consistent, scorecard-driven session.

An employee who values their reputation will not refer someone they expect to fail. That implicit filter shifts the base rate of quality candidates upward before any assessment is administered.

When every interviewer uses the same scorecard, consensus is faster because everyone rates the same dimensions. Offer-stage dropout falls because candidates have not been subjected to five disconnected conversations asking variations of the same question.

According to Gallup’s State of the Global Workplace , only 20% of employees worldwide are engaged at work, with disengagement costing an estimated $10 trillion in lost productivity globally. Engagement problems often trace back to hiring: a wrong-fit hire who stays is more expensive than one who leaves at 90 days.

According to Gallup’s meta-analysis on employee engagement , highly engaged teams show 43% lower turnover and 23% higher profitability than their disengaged peers. The cost reduction goal and the quality goal are the same.
cards.heading: How do referrals and structured interviews reduce talent acquisition costs?

cards.gloss: Recommends tracking cost per hire, quality of hire, and time to fill together to confirm real (not deferred) savings.
cards.verbatim: Track three metrics together: cost per hire, quality of hire measured by 90-day performance and retention, and time to fill. A genuine cost reduction shows falling cost per hire alongside stable or improving quality of hire.
cards.heading: How do you measure whether recruitment cost reduction is working?

cards.gloss: Defines each of the three metrics precisely and warns against optimizing cost per hire alone while missing attrition signals.
cards.verbatim:
Cost per hire equals total recruiting spend divided by total hires in the period. Benchmark internally before comparing to industry figures, which vary too much by sector and seniority to be directly useful.

Quality of hire equals 90-day retention rate plus early performance scores from managers. This is the metric that reveals whether your cost reduction is real or deferred.

Time to fill measures calendar days from role open to offer accepted. Improvements here confirm that your process changes are working end to end, not just reducing spend on one line item while slowing everything else.

Running all three together prevents the most common mistake in TA cost management: optimizing cost per hire in isolation and missing the attrition signal that arrives in the next quarter’s data.

A screen-first hiring process, supported by structured assessments, referrals, and data-driven decision-making, turns recruitment from a cost center into a predictable investment.

What is a typical cost per hire for enterprise companies? 

Gallup research puts the cost of replacing a single employee at between half and twice their annual salary. For a senior role paying $80,000, that range is $40,000-$160,000 per restart. That is why preventing bad hires matters as much as reducing initial sourcing spend.

 How much can pre-employment assessments reduce interview volume?

 What is the ROI of a structured employee referral program? 

A referral bonus of $500-$1,500 per successful hire compares to an agency fee of 15-25% of first-year salary. For a role paying $60,000, that is a $9,000-$15,000 saving per hire versus an agency placement, one of the highest-ROI investments in any TA budget.

 Do structured interviews reduce time to hire or just improve quality? 

Both. When every interviewer uses the same scorecard, consensus happens faster and one round often replaces three. That cuts 5-10 days off the average time to fill, while also reducing offer-stage dropout from candidates frustrated by a slow, inconsistent process.

cards.gloss: TL;DR summary: ROI formula, the KPI categories to track, why quality of hire matters most, and how to benchmark against your own trend.
cards.verbatim:
- Talent acquisition ROI compares recruiting cost against the value, retention, and performance of the people you hire. 
- The core formula is simple: value gained from a hire, minus the cost to hire them, divided by that cost. 
- Track a small set of KPIs that span cost, speed, quality, and retention. Quality of hire is the one that protects ROI the most. 
- Cost and speed are easy to count but easy to game. A cheap, fast hire who quits in six months wipes out the saving. 
- Benchmark against your own trend first, then industry data. A skills assessment before the first interview gives quality of hire a number you can defend.
cards.heading: TL;DR

cards.gloss: Gives the ROI formula (value gained minus cost, divided by cost), explains the cost-per-hire side via the ANSI/SHRM standard, and notes value must be estimated with proxies.
cards.verbatim:
The basic formula is the same one you would use for any investment:

 Talent acquisition ROI = (Value gained from the hire – Cost to hire) / Cost to hire, shown as a percentage 

The cost side is the easy part. Add internal recruiting costs and external ones over the same period, then divide by hires made. That is the ANSI/SHRM cost-per-hire standard , and it lands U.S. employers at about $4,700 a hire on average. SHRM also notes the fully loaded cost of a hire can reach three to four times the position’s salary once you count soft costs like manager time, so a $60,000 role can cost $180,000 or more to fill. Roughly 30% to 40% of that is hard cost; the other 60% is soft cost you rarely see on an invoice.

The value side is harder, and that is where most ROI math falls apart. You cannot put an exact dollar figure on every hire, so use proxies: revenue per employee for sales roles, output or tickets closed for operational roles, and retention for everyone. The point is not false precision. It is a consistent method you apply the same way every quarter, so the trend is honest even if the absolute number is an estimate.
cards.heading: How do you calculate talent acquisition ROI?

cards.gloss: Breaks total cost to hire into hard costs (30-40%, invoiced items) and soft costs (60%, recruiter/manager time and ramp-up), totaling ~$180,000 for a $60,000 role.
cards.verbatim: The denominator in your ROI formula has two layers that SHRM separates clearly. Hard costs (30-40% of total) are the ones on invoices: job board spend, agency fees, assessment tools, and background checks. Soft costs (roughly 60%) are the ones that never appear on a vendor invoice: recruiter hours, hiring manager interview time, and the productivity ramp while a new hire gets up to speed. Add both layers and a $60,000 role costs roughly $180,000 to fill when you count everything.
cards.heading: What goes into the total cost to hire?

cards.gloss: Worked numeric example calculating ROI for a customer success hire (210% good-hire case vs. -45% if the hire leaves at six months).
cards.verbatim:
Role: a mid-level customer success manager at a $70,000 annual salary. Hard recruiting costs run to $21,000 (30% of salary, per SHRM’s cost-per-hire benchmarks). Soft costs – hiring manager interview time, onboarding coordination, and the first 30 days of reduced productivity – add another $14,000. Total cost to hire: $35,000.

The role sat open for 38 days. SHRM’s 2022 Human Capital Benchmarking Report puts average time to fill at 42 days for professional roles, so 38 days is typical. At $70,000 per year, each unfilled working day costs roughly $269 in lost output (annual salary divided by 260 working days). Vacancy cost: $10,200. Total investment: $45,200.

In year one, the hire retains and expands an account portfolio worth $140,000 in revenue – a conservative two-times salary multiple for a customer success role. Talent acquisition ROI = ($140,000 – $45,200) / $45,200 = 210% . For every dollar spent recruiting this hire, the business returned $3.10.

Now run the bad-hire version. Same $45,200 cost to hire. Hire leaves at month six. Year-one value drops to $70,000 (half the output, half the year). You incur a replacement cost of $45,200 a second time. Total cost: $90,400. Net value: $70,000 – $90,400 = -$20,400. ROI: -45% . One early exit flips a 210% return into a loss. That is the arithmetic case for measuring quality of hire.
cards.heading: Worked example: what talent acquisition ROI looks like with real numbers

cards.gloss: Table of core TA KPIs (cost per hire, time to fill, time to hire, quality of hire, retention, offer acceptance, source effectiveness) with what each measures and how to read it.
cards.verbatim:
You do not need 30 metrics. You need a handful that span cost, speed, quality, and retention, and you need to read them together. A KPI on its own lies. Cost per hire dropped? Great, unless quality dropped with it. Here are the ones worth tracking.

 Metric 
 What it measures

 Cost per hire Total recruiting spend divided by hires made Lower is good only if quality holds. U.S. average is near $4,700.

cards.heading: Which talent acquisition metrics and KPIs actually matter?

cards.gloss: Explains why cost per hire and time to fill are easy to game and should never be used alone without quality signals.
cards.verbatim: Cost per hire and time to fill are the metrics everyone starts with, because they are simple to count. That is also their weakness. They measure effort and speed, not outcome. A recruiter can cut both by lowering the bar, and the numbers will look better right up until the new hire underperforms or quits. Use them, but never alone.
cards.heading: Cost per hire and time to fill: the easy ones

cards.gloss: Details quality of hire as the metric that drives ROI, citing LinkedIn 2025 survey stats, and recommends a blended pre-hire assessment + manager rating + retention score.
cards.verbatim:
Quality of hire is the metric that actually moves return on investment, and it is the one teams find hardest to pin down. It blends three signals: first-year performance ratings, retention past probation, and hiring-manager satisfaction with the match. In LinkedIn’s 2025 Future of Recruiting report (a survey of more than 1,000 talent pros), 93% said accurately assessing a candidate’s skills is central to improving quality of hire, and 61% believe AI can help them measure it better.

This is the gap a skills assessment closes. When a candidate takes a role-based test before the first interview, you get a baseline score you can compare against their later performance. That turns quality of hire from a gut feeling into a number, which is the only way to improve quality of hire on purpose rather than by luck.

 Pro Tip: Score quality of hire on a 1-to-5 scale that combines a pre-hire assessment result, a 90-day manager rating, and one-year retention. One blended number per hire makes the metric easy to trend, and easy to defend when finance asks what recruiting returned.
cards.heading: Quality of hire: the one that decides ROI

cards.gloss: Argues TA ROI matters because replacement cost of a bad hire (0.5-2x salary) dwarfs cost per hire, so teams should optimize quality over shaving hiring costs.
cards.verbatim:
Because hiring is one of the largest controllable costs in any people-heavy business, and most of it is invisible. The danger is not the obvious spend; it is the bad hire you have to replace. SHRM research puts the cost of replacing one employee at one-half to two times their annual salary. At a $70,000 average salary, that is a $35,000 to $140,000 replacement cost per departure – and that is before counting the productivity gap while the seat sits open.

Put those two numbers next to each other. A $4,700 cost per hire looks tiny against a replacement cost that can hit two times salary. So the team that obsesses over shaving $500 off cost per hire, while ignoring a quality problem that causes early exits, is optimizing the wrong end. That is the core argument for measuring ROI: it stops you from saving pennies on recruiting while burning dollars on turnover.
cards.heading: Why does talent acquisition ROI matter to the business?

cards.gloss: Explains how ATS/analytics cut cost and pre-hire assessments raise quality, with a concrete example of a software company compressing time to fill via coding assessments.
cards.verbatim:
Technology lifts ROI in two places: it cuts the cost and time of screening, and it raises the quality of who gets through. An applicant tracking system and recruiting analytics handle the first. Pre-hire skills assessments handle the second, and the second is where the bigger ROI sits, because quality of hire is what protects you from replacement cost.

Here is a concrete version. A 500-person software company hiring 20 engineers a quarter sends a coding assessment before any recruiter screen. The shortlist arrives already scored, so the first human conversation happens with candidates who can actually do the work. SHRM benchmarks average time to fill at 42 days for professional roles. A screening loop that used to run six weeks compresses to about ten days, and the interviewers stop spending time on people who were never going to pass the technical bar. Lower cost per hire and higher quality of hire, from the same change.

The catch, and there is always a catch, is that an assessment is only as good as its fit to the role. A generic test bolted onto a specialized job adds noise, not signal. Match the test to the actual work, and pair it with assessment data you actually review , or you are just adding a step.
cards.heading: How does technology improve talent acquisition ROI?

cards.gloss: Recommends benchmarking your own quarter-over-quarter trend first, then using industry averages only as context for questions, not as targets.
cards.verbatim:
Start with yourself, not the industry. Your own quarter-over-quarter trend is the most honest benchmark you have, because it controls for your roles, your market, and your pay bands. Pull three or four quarters of cost per hire, time to fill, quality of hire, and retention, and look at the direction of travel before you compare to anyone else.

Then bring in external numbers carefully. Industry averages like the $4,700 cost per hire are useful context, but they hide huge variation. A senior engineering hire in a tight market and a high-volume support hire are not the same line item, and an average blends them into a figure that fits neither. Use benchmarks to ask questions (why is our cost double the average for this role?), not to set targets you then game.

 Key Takeaway: ROI is a trend, not a trophy. One clean quarter proves nothing. The teams that improve hiring are the ones that read cost, speed, quality, and retention together, every quarter, and act on the one metric that is dragging the rest.
cards.heading: How do you benchmark talent acquisition ROI?

cards.gloss: Describes the 'Testlify ROI Scorecard' quarterly loop: baseline, score quality pre-interview, connect the KPIs, and act on the weakest metric.
cards.verbatim:
The answer is a consistent quarterly review loop. We call ours the Testlify ROI Scorecard. Four steps, run every quarter, it keeps the focus on the metric that matters instead of the one that is easiest to count.

- Baseline. Record cost per hire, time to fill, quality of hire, and retention for the last full quarter. This is your starting line. 
- Score quality before the interview. Run a role-based skills assessment up front, so every candidate gets a comparable quality score, not a resume guess. 
- Connect the numbers. Track each KPI together. If cost drops but quality or retention drops with it, the saving is not real. 
- Act on the weakest link. Fix the one metric dragging ROI down, then re-baseline next quarter. Repeat. 

None of this needs a data-science team. It needs a consistent method and a quality signal you trust. For more on the analytics side, our guide to analytics for smarter hiring goes deeper on the reporting setup.
cards.heading: How do you track talent acquisition ROI quarter over quarter?

cards.gloss: FAQ answering what counts as good ROI, how to calculate cost per hire, the difference between time to fill and time to hire, and how to measure quality of hire.
cards.verbatim:
What is a good ROI for talent acquisition? 

There is no single magic number, because it depends on the role and industry. A practical target is a recruiting spend that returns several times its cost through faster productive hiring, lower turnover, and stronger performance. Track the trend in your own cost per hire and quality of hire over time, then compare each new quarter against your own baseline rather than a generic benchmark.

 How do you calculate cost per hire? 

Add your internal recruiting costs (recruiter salaries, referral payouts) and external costs (job ads, agency fees, assessment tools) over a set period, then divide by the number of hires in that same period. This is the ANSI/SHRM standard formula , and SHRM put the U.S. average at nearly $4,700 per hire.

 What is the difference between time to fill and time to hire? 

Time to fill counts the days from when a job opens to when an offer is accepted, so it measures pipeline and process speed. Time to hire counts the days from when a candidate enters your pipeline to when they accept, so it measures how fast you move a single person through. Track both: one tells you about demand, the other about your funnel.

 How do you measure quality of hire? 

Quality of hire blends a few signals: first-year job performance ratings, new-hire retention past the probation period, and hiring-manager satisfaction with the match. A skills assessment taken before the first interview gives you a baseline score to compare against later performance, which is why 93% of talent pros told LinkedIn that accurately assessing skills is central to improving quality of hire.

 Which talent acquisition metric matters most? 

Quality of hire. Speed and cost are easy to count, but a cheap, fast hire who leaves in six months destroys ROI. SHRM research puts the cost of replacing one employee at one-half to two times their annual salary, so the metric that protects you from a bad hire is the one worth defending in a budget review.

cards.gloss: How to reduce time-to-hire by identifying which pipeline stage (screening, interview gaps, offer approval) consumes the most time and targeting that stage first.
cards.verbatim:
The US average time to hire reached 44 days in 2026 according to SHRM. For an enterprise filling 200 roles per year, every week above that baseline represents direct cost in delayed productivity and extended contractor spend. Recruitment analytics makes time reduction systematic rather than incidental.
Start by mapping where time is lost in the pipeline. Most hiring delays concentrate in three places: time from application to first screen, time between interview stages, and time from final interview to offer. Analytics makes those delays visible at the stage level so the team can address the right constraint. The most common and most expensive mistake is optimizing the wrong stage – many teams invest in sourcing velocity when the actual delay is internal approval cycles, and without stage-level data that diagnosis error is invisible.
A useful starting exercise: pull the last quarter’s hiring data and calculate the median elapsed time at each stage. Rank stages by total days consumed. cards.gloss: Describes three layers of pipeline analytics maturity (funnel data, assessment-to-screen signal, assessment-to-outcome linkage) and introduces Testlify's Recruitment Analytics Scorecard framework.
cards.verbatim:
Most ATS analytics track funnel velocity: how many candidates advance at each stage, how long each stage takes, where drop-off occurs. That data describes process speed. It does not explain why some hires succeed and others leave within the first year.
Skills assessment data adds the predictive layer. When structured pre-employment tests are run consistently across every hire in a role family, the result is a dataset that connects candidate capabilities at the point of screening to actual job performance months later. Over time – typically after 500 or more hires in a role type – that dataset identifies which skill dimensions are genuinely predictive vs. which ones feel important but have no relationship to outcomes.
This is the foundation of Testlify’s Recruitment Analytics Scorecard: a role-specific framework that benchmarks assessment cut-scores against verified hire outcomes at 90 days and 12 months.
Layer 1 – Baseline funnel analytics: Time to hire, source of hire, pipeline conversion rates by stage. Most enterprise teams have this layer in some form.
Layer 2 – Assessment-to-screen signal quality: Which test score ranges produce candidates who convert to offer at higher rates. Fewer teams have this layer.
Layer 3 – Assessment-to-outcome linkage: Which score profiles predict 12-month performance and retention. Almost no team has this layer without a structured assessment program feeding their analytics system.
The pipeline implication: every candidate who passes a screen is a data point. Every hire outcome is a follow-up data point. Connecting those two points is where the most actionable pipeline intelligence lives. Data lives in too many places. Sourcing data sits in LinkedIn, pipeline data in the ATS, assessment data in a separate platform, performance data in the HRIS. The practical fix is not replacing all four systems. It is building a lightweight data pipeline that extracts four key metrics – time to hire, source of hire, assessment score, first-year performance – into one shared view. A spreadsheet updated weekly beats a perfect data warehouse that will be ready next quarter.
Nobody owns the analysis. When analytics is everyone’s responsibility, it becomes nobody’s in practice. Designating one person – a recruiting operations lead or a senior recruiter – to own the weekly metrics review and flag anomalies changes the outcome. That person does not need to be a data scientist. They need to ask “why did this number change?” every week and route the answer to the person who can act on it.
The data is not connected to decisions. Analytics that produces a report no one acts on is decoration. The test: can the recruiting team name one hiring decision made differently in the last 30 days because of something the analytics showed? cards.gloss: Walks through a formula and steps for calculating ROI on a recruitment analytics investment, including baselining, setting targets, valuing time saved, and modeling returns over 3 years.
cards.verbatim:
ROI on recruitment analytics is measurable, but most teams never calculate it because they do not establish a baseline before implementation. The formula is straightforward: ROI = (Cost savings from analytics improvements + Revenue impact of faster hiring) / Cost of analytics investment.
- Establish a baseline. Document current cost per hire, time to hire, first-year attrition rate, and offer acceptance rate before beginning a structured analytics program. Without a baseline, improvement cannot be quantified.
- Set improvement targets against benchmarks. If SHRM shows a US median time to hire of 44 days and the current state is 58 days, a 20% reduction to 46 days is a defensible initial target tied to an external standard.
- Assign a value per day. For revenue-generating roles, each day unfilled carries a calculable productivity cost. For support roles, use replacement cost – typically 50-150% of annual salary per SHRM data. At a conservative $8,000 average replacement cost per hire, filling 200 roles 5 days faster generates $1.6M in annual value.
- Compare against investment. Set the productivity gain against the cost of the analytics toolset and program management. An analytics investment of $200K against $1.6M in time-to-hire savings alone represents an 8:1 return in Year 1, before factoring in attrition reduction.
- Model on a 3-year horizon. The quality-of-hire prediction models that take 12-18 months to build compound in value over time. The 15-25% attrition reduction from assessment-to-outcome linkage grows with every cohort of hires. CFO presentations should show a 3-year ROI curve, not a 12-month payback.

Hiring is expensive, but the highest costs rarely appear on your recruitment budget. Most companies track job ads, recruiter fees, and interview expenses, yet overlook the hidden costs of vacant roles, lost productivity, manager time, and poor hiring decisions. Those indirect costs often exceed the price of recruitment itself.
Understanding the difference between direct and indirect hiring costs is the first step toward controlling your cost per hire and improving your recruiting ROI. In this guide, you’ll learn what each type of hiring cost includes, how to calculate them accurately, and practical ways to reduce both without sacrificing hiring quality or speed.
TL;DR
- Direct hiring costs are visible and invoiced (job ads, agency fees, background checks, assessments, signing bonus). Indirect costs are hidden (recruiter and interviewer time, lost productivity, onboarding, a bad hire).
- SHRM puts the average cost per hire at about $4,700, but that mostly counts direct costs. Add indirect costs and the real total often runs two to three times higher.
- The most expensive indirect cost is a wrong hire. Gallup estimates replacing an employee costs 50% to 200% of their annual salary.
- Most salaries are indirect costs, because they support the business broadly rather than one traceable task.

Direct hiring costs are the expenses you can point to on a receipt. They attach to one hire and one recruitment cycle, which makes them the easiest part of the budget to forecast. The common ones:

Indirect hiring costs are the less visible expenses that arise during the hiring process and after a role remains unfilled. They include lost productivity, manager and recruiter time, delayed projects, overtime for existing employees, slower onboarding, and the impact of a poor hire.
Unlike direct costs, these expenses do not appear on an invoice, but they can have a much greater effect on business performance.

cards.gloss: Lists examples of indirect hiring costs: lost productivity, recruiter/interviewer time, onboarding, admin overhead, lower morale, and the outsized cost of a bad hire (citing Gallup's 50-200% of salary estimate).

Indirect hiring costs are the expenses that never reach an invoice but still hit the bottom line. They come from the time and attention hiring pulls away from the rest of the business, and from the fallout when a hire goes wrong. The big ones:
- Lost productivity: Output dips while a role sits open and again while a new hire ramps, because experienced people split their time to cover and to train.
- Recruiter and interviewer time: The hours HR and your top performers spend reviewing resumes, running interviews, and scoring candidates.
- Onboarding and training: Orientation, tools, and the ramp period before a new hire is fully productive.
- Admin overhead: Payroll setup, benefits enrollment, equipment, and records work for each new person.
- Lower morale: An understaffed, overworked team gets stressed and disengaged, which can trigger more resignations and more vacancies.
- A bad hire: When a hire doesn’t work out, the costs extend far beyond recruiting again. You pay for lost productivity, additional training, separation costs, and the time needed to refill the role. Gallup estimates that replacing an employee costs 50% to 200% of their annual salary.

Recruitment metrics are the numbers that tell you whether your hiring is working: how fast you fill roles, what each hire costs, where your best people come from, and how well they perform once they start. Track them in real time and hiring stops being a guessing game. You see a bottleneck the week it appears, not in a quarterly report when the role is already cold.
Most teams still review hiring data after the fact. That is the problem. By the time a monthly dashboard shows that a job has been open for 60 days, the strong candidates have taken other offers. This guide covers the eight recruitment metrics worth watching as they move, how to read each one, and how to turn them into faster, fairer decisions in 2026.
